subtopic: CANADIAN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY- STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN DEEP-SEA SHIPPING INDUSTRY- STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a declaration of government policy with respect to the Canadian merchant marine.
During recent months the government has been giving very serious and careful consideration to the state of the Canadian deep-sea shipping industry. The main facts of the situation are fully set forth in the report of the Canadian maritime commission; since that report was prepared an increasing number of Canadian flag ships have been laid up. The government proposes to deal with the matter promptly.
The problem stated in simple terms is this. Canadian flag vessels are no longer able to pay their own way. This situation is not new. Not since the beginning of this century has the business of owning and operating deep-sea vessels really prospered in Canada. In fact from 1900 to 1919 there was very little Canadian participation in deep-sea shipping. However, the building of ships in Canada during the first world war led the government of that day into a post-war venture of a government-owned merchant fleet. That fleet proved to be uncompetitive in the world market, and when the Canadian government merchant marine was finally liquidated in 45781-189
1936, the total loss to the government, exclusive of interest on capital and other advances, amounted to over $82 million.
During the second world war it again became necessary for Canada to build ships to carry essential supplies. In 1946 the Canadian merchant fleet was the fourth largest in the world. The Canadian government at that time, instead of continuing to operate a government-owned fleet in a period of high freights, decided to dispose of its vessels.
In 1946 there was a strong demand for ships both in Canada and abroad. Companies in Canada were most anxious to purchase ships, and under these circumstances it appeared only right and proper to give to our own people the first opportunity to buy. Thus the bulk of the war-built fleet was sold to Canadian operators at reasonable prices and on favourable terms, but they purchased these vessels at their own risk. On the 16th day of June, 1947, my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), in addressing this house said:
Hon. members are well aware that a merchant navy is basically an industry which, like other industries, has to pay its way if it is to survive.
During the years 1946 and 1947 ocean freight rates remained at high levels and Canadian owners were able to operate their vessels profitably and successfully. About the middle of 1948, however, Canadian ships began to experience greater difficulty in obtaining dollar cargoes and freight rates began to decline from their high wartime levels. In March of this year a steady decline set in which has continued and at present rates and at Canadian costs Canadian vessels cannot be operated without substantial losses.
As I have said, the Canadian government has sold all its ships, the majority of which have been purchased by Canadian owners. At the present time we have 118 dry-cargo vessels operating under Canadian flag, and an additional 58, which likewise have been sold, are due to be returned from United Kingdom flag to Canadian registry next year, making a total of 176 ships which we must take into consideration. I am advised that, in order to enable those ships to operate competitively in the world market, over $25 million in annual subsidies would be required.
The maintenance of a Canadian flag merchant fleet can be justified only on the basis of one or both of two assumptions: (1) that

Merchant Marine
the fleet is a net economic asset to the community, or (2) that the fleet is important for purposes of national security.
In considering the studies which are available to us on the subject, we have concluded that we are not justified from an economic viewpoint in maintaining a Canadian flag fleet by artificial means. It is not the intention of the government to maintain an industry at the expense of the taxpayer, and of other export industries, by the unhealthy method of subsidies, unless these countervailing considerations are very strong indeed.
There are many objections to shipping subsidies. They do not tend to promote a healthy and efficient industry. They constitute a steady and usually increasing drain upon public funds. In a world in which some types of ships are already in oversupply they represent a waste of the taxpayer's money.
I do not propose to go into all the difficulties involved in shipping subsidies, since the government's basic objection to a policy of subsidization rests on wider grounds. The world is still suffering from the effect of two great wars. Dislocation resulting from such wars has disrupted world trade to an extent that nations are taking extraordinary steps for the preservation of their economies. Our view has consistently been that it is not possible to seek a solution to our trade and currency difficulties on a purely national basis. Canada has goods to sell, but our European customers lack dollars to buy them. They cannot acquire such dollars unless we do our share of buying from them. In other words we must seek to encourage imports from countries to whom we desire to sell our goods and in this sense shipping services of other countries represent an import. We must not adopt measures which would hinder the revival of world trade and defer the achievement of balance between dollar and non-dollar trading areas. If we were to adopt a policy of subsidization of national shipping, it would be a protectionist measure disabling other countries from trading with us.
The problem of preserving some part of the fleet for national security purposes deserves further consideration. In a world at peace with itself, this would not be necessary. Each nation would perform those functions which it could carry out most efficiently and economically, and if Canada were unable to conduct deep-sea shipping operations as well as other countries, such operations would be abandoned. Safeguards would have to be set up to prevent countries engaged in shipping from discriminating against countries which had no shipping.

However, we must regard the world as it is and make a realistic approach to the problem.
Safeguards to prevent discrimination have been set up under the machinery of the United Nations, and the constitution of the intergovernmental maritime consultative organization is designed to prevent unfair shipping practices. But although Canada has ratified the IMCO convention, it has not yet received the agreement of sufficient nations to bring it into operation. Furthermore, unhappily, we cannot say that war is not a possibility. I am strongly of the opinion, however, that arrangements should be made between the peace-loving nations of the world to pool their shipping resources in the event of war. If proper assurances were received in this respect, it might not be necessary for those nations who cannot operate ships economically to continue to maintain merchant fleets to meet an emergency.
The maintenance of adequate ocean-going shipping, shipbuilding capacity and ship repair facilities is fundamental to the defence organization of the North Atlantic treaty. It is, like defence proper, a collective responsibility which the partners must share in relation to capacity, aptitude, and relative efficiency. An increasing degree of specialization along the lines in which each country can make the greatest contribution to the common defence and welfare is the natural complement of the principle of integration in defence planning which we, together with our partners in the North Atlantic treaty, have accepted and have begun to apply. The implications of this approach are plain.
The experience of two wars has made it plain that allies have to pool their shipping resources. This lesson has not been lost on the countries which are now associated, for purposes of common defence, in the North Atlantic treaty. It is our hope, to further which we shall use our best endeavours, that arrangements can be completed in peacetime which would ensure the prompt, fair and efficient use and allocation of all available shipping in any emergency. Conversations to this end are already under way. In particular, discussions on this subject have taken place between officials of the government of the United Kingdom and Canada. Those discussions have not yet been completed, but I believe that if Canadian ships are transferred to United Kingdom registry, arrangements can be made to treat such ships as part of the Canadian contribution to any allied shipping pool in the event of war. Similar conditions would govern any transfer of registry for operating purposes to the flags of other countries upon whose close co-operation in mutual defence we can confidently

rely. By proceeding along these lines and within the framework of security which we are building up, it should no longer be necessary for each individual country to risk the waste of its national effort in duplicating facilities and services which can be more efficiently carried out in peacetime by their partner countries, and which will be available to serve the needs of all should a war come.
The government has therefore decided that, for the next year-and I stress "for the next year"-while an allied defence shipping pool is being created, it is advisable to maintain some proportion of the present fleet under Canadian flag. For that purpose the government has decided to recommend the provision of a sum of $3 million as an aid to the Canadian ocean shipping industry for one year only. It is estimated that over 500,000 deadweight tons of dry-cargo shipping will remain under the Canadian flag, but it may be that not all vessels comprising that tonnage will receive assistance. The number of ships to be assisted, and the amount of assistance required by each, will be left to the Canadian maritime commission, who will administer the fund under the provisions of the act, if parliament sees fit to pass it.
It is recognized that the reduction contemplated in the fleet will compel a number of seamen to find shore employment. In order to assist them in this transfer, the government has decided to extend the vocational training scheme to admit eligible men applying on or before the 30th day of September, 1950, and commencing their approved training before the 31st day of January, 1951. The ministers of transport and veterans affairs will have discretion with regard to the restricting provisions respecting age and the granting of allowances as at present set out in the merchant seamen vocational training order. Hon. members know that the terms of that order restricted training to men under thirty years of age.

speechtext:
That is to remain the rule; but there will be discretionary provisions enabling the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Transport in exceptional cases to extend the privilege to men who have passed the age of thirty.
The vessels of the Park fleet, which, I have said, were sold by the government to Canadian companies, were purchased under the terms of an agreement containing the following clause:

-the vessels sold will be operated under Canadian registry by the purchaser as well after as before the full balance of the final or adjusted purchase price and interest has been paid; and the purchaser agrees for itself, its successors and assigns, not to make any application for transfer of any of the vessels out of Canadian registry without the prior written approval of the seller.
If it had not been for this clause, Canadian companies could have transferred their ships to foreign flag at any time. That covenant has now been in force for about four years, and it is now felt, in view of what I have said, that it is fair to give relief in respect of this restriction, as it has been demonstrated that Canadian vessels with their present high costs cannot be operated. Applications from shipowners may now be made to the Minister of Transport, through the commission, to transfer flag, and transfers will be permitted under such conditions as he may impose. This is in conformity with what I said previously about the concern to have an arrangement for a shipping pool that would give us the confidence that ships would be available in the event of an emergency.
Such transfer of flag, of itself, does not of course affect the ownership of the vessels, which will remain in Canadian hands. In permitting transfers the government will see to it that there will be tonnage available to meet Canadian needs in the event of war, and it is hoped that by means of such transfers Canadian-owned vessels will be able to secure cargoes which have not been available to them by reason of currency restrictions.
Let me emphasize again that the relief which is now being granted to the shipping industry is temporary and for one year only. It is given to assist shipowners to meet the emergency created by the decline in the freight market, and in the hope that they will be able to reduce their costs in order to operate competitively.
May I take this opportunity to pay a tribute, which I think all hon. members would wish to pay, to the efficient and intelligent work which has been done by the maritime commission, under the chairmanship of Mr. Clyne, in coping with a most difficult and somewhat discouraging problem under the conditions which prevailed when they had to give all their time and energy in an attempt to find a solution to that problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset of this sitting of the committee I should like to raise a question of privilege.
Before the resignation of the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act becomes effective, he is endeavouring to complete two reports which he now has in the course of preparation. In this connection he has asked me, with regard to the first of the two reports, whether I would approve of getting out 100 odd copies of it, not printed but in mimeographed form. He said this was


the only way in which we could get the report published within the statutory period of fifteen days. He said if we did not publish it in mimeographed form we would not be able to get it published within fifteen days after its delivery to the minister. I asked him, if it was necessary to mimeograph on the present occasion, how it had been possible in the past to comply with the requirement that reports be published within fifteen days. Mr. McGregor then informed me for the first time that the combines investigation commission, and the ministers responsible for it in previous years, had had a great deal of trouble in complying with the section, and as a matter of fact had always found that if a printed report was to be published it was mechanically impossible to comply with it. He said that even when the report went from him in first-class order to a minister who knew all about its preparation, and who had been kept fully informed by him of its various stages, it had not been possible to accomplish publication of the printed report within the statutory period of fifteen days. This has happened not through any lack of attention or effort on his part, or through any indisposition of the minister to publish, but simply because the fifteen days provided in the act is too short.
In view of all the criticism that has been heaped upon me, some of it going to the extreme length of hinting that, like Charles I, I should be beheaded for this grave offence, I would ask members of the press gallery to give due publicity to the point I am now raising. That I should have raised it before in my argument I do not for a moment deny, but this is just another example of the position in which I have found myself from beginning to end in this matter. That is, having no direct knowledge of the matter which has been under discussion, I have been continually under the necessity of securing all the information I have required in these debates from other people, mainly civil servants; and having heard no suggestion at any time that the act should be amended to extend this period of fifteen days to a more realistic period, naturally I assumed that it had been found to be satisfactory. That is one reason why there was no provision in the bill brought down this session to extend that period. That is also why, in addressing ourselves to the matter of the publication of this report which has not yet been delivered to me, the commissioner and I have to put our heads together to devise unusual ways and means of managing to comply with the statutory requirement of publishing within fifteen days.

In my own case I was not the minister who was familiar with this matter. I came in as a new minister, totally unfamiliar with either the flour report or any of the matters out of which it had arisen, and found on my desk an accumulation of some six weeks' arrears of work, with the session to prepare for, and with a flour report in respect of which the period for publication was known to be completely inadequate but as to which the statutory period of fifteen days began to run some five days before I even got here.
I think I can say with reasonable modesty that I came to this city with a good name, which it had taken me twenty-two years of hard, diligent work in the public service to build up. There are those in this house who would take it from me because I did not comply within ten days with a provision which, as the records show, on several occasions it has been quite impossible to comply with in the fifteen day period.
Nor within ten months.

I do not
think anyone in this house was at any time attacking the good name of the Minister of Justice. Those of us who know him particularly well, including myself, a political opponent from Manitoba, have always paid tribute to his fairness and other very admirable qualities. If there is criticism directed to him it is not because he is Stuart Garson but because he is the Minister of Justice, and one who broke the law of this country.
I must say that I find his statement today singularly unconvincing. There has been criticism of the minister and the government, and I think that criticism is well merited, because justice in this country must be even-handed and impartial. Justice must apply to those in positions of power and prominence as well as to those in more humble walks of life; and the minister has broken the law. I do not say he has defied it; I say he has broken it. If fifteen days is not long enough, then we shall have to amend the act; but the law states that the period is fifteen days. I think most hon. members would go further and agree that the fifteen days should run from that date toward the end of February when the last amendment was made.
What are the chronological facts of the situation? The report was presented last December. I think it should be said in fairness to the minister, though he has not said it himself, that when that report was presented he was lying in bed in Manitoba,
Supply-Justice
a very sick man. Therefore he could not have been expected to know what was in the report. Nevertheless there must have been an acting minister at that time. A few days later, I believe, Mr. McGregor sent in a request for authorization to print the report. That authorization was not granted until some time in April. I believe the report was printed before the last parliament was dissolved; yet members of that parliament never saw it.
I point out that the minister has broken the law. There is a punishment in Canada for those who break the law. I must admit that I am not fully conversant with the law, not being a lawyer, but still I can read certain aspects of it. I maintain that the minister did not comply with the law; and here I speak of the Minister of Justice. In that case section 164 of the Criminal Code must apply, and that section reads:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment who, without lawful excuse, disobeys any act of the parliament of Canada or of any legislature in Canada by wilfully doing any act which it forbids, or omitting to do any act which it requires to be done, unless some penalty or other mode of punishment is expressly provided by law.
I hope the minister will realize that, to use the familiar cliche of the Minister of Labour, I am speaking in a kindly way, you understand. I do not want to see the Minister of Justice go to jail for Christmas; but if he does have to go to jail I suggest that he invoke section 574 of the Criminal Code and take some of his colleagues with him. That section deals with accessories after the fact, and reads:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to seven years' imprisonment-
This is more severe than the other section. -who, in any case where no express provision is made by this act for the punishment of an accessory, is accessory after the fact to any indictable offence for which the punishment is, on a first conviction, imprisonment for life-
Perhaps that is the wrong section. In any case I suggest that the minister's colleagues are liable to be sent down for about seven years for being accessories with him. There might have been a general disposition to feel that this matter had been adequately dealt with in the earlier discussions had it not been for the extraordinary statement made today by the Minister of Justice. He now seeks to suggest that the criticism which has been directed in this chamber to the procedure followed was improper. He speaks of his reputation, and

Supply-Justice
suggests that people would take it from him. The implication is that those who have clearly stated what were the requirements of the law had some motive other than to place before this house the necessity of obeying fundamental and well-established principles of our parliamentary system and the responsibility of government to parliament. The minister comes in at this late hour, unrepentant, and even taking away any limited measure of regret that he expressed previously. Now he says that Mr. McGregor indicates that it will be necessary to have another report, which Mr. McGregor is completing, mimeographed if there is to be compliance with the law requiring publication within fifteen days; that that requirement is something with which it has not been practicable to comply all along. Did the commissioner say to the Minister of Justice that it takes ten and a half months to do it? Did he say to the Minister of Justice: You should amend the time within which publication takes place and be sure to allow ten months, because that is the time required? Unless that was said, then all this is meaningless. It does not make clear the elaborate and detailed explanation given by the Minister of Justice for the ten months' delay in complying with this requirement.
The fact is that on the basis of what the minister says this morning there could have been compliance with the act. The only requirement is that there be publication. There is not a word about printing. It is simply a matter of providing the material upon which the report can be published. This being so, the suggestion of the necessity for mimeographing imposes no limitation; it demonstrates the extent to which the minister feels it is necessary to go to explain what he did, rather than apologize for what he did. The suggestion conveyed, not in words but by implication, is that there was no substantial ground for the criticism which has been directed to the conduct of the minister and the members of the government who joined in this extraordinary procedure.
In the closing hours of this session, let the Minister of Justice not come to us and say that the delay in this case was the result of any procedural or mimeographing difficulty, when he spent such a long time explaining exactly why he had not published the report. In a nutshell, the story is that he examined the report and discussed it with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not willing to let it be published. As a result of the objection raised by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, publication did not take place. That is the explanation, and not that fifteen days

was not enough time. Then there were discussions with the officials, and the Minister of Justice explained that on different occasions he brought other senior officials and Mr. McGregor together, so that they could reconcile their points of view, if possible, in regard to this important matter. All that had nothing to do with any difficulty in complying with the requirement that publication shall take place within fifteen days.
If there had not been any great reason for concern before this morning, Mr. Chairman, about the measure of responsibility displayed by the government in regard to obligations of this kind, there is now, having regard to the explanation given this morning by the Minister of Justice. After reviewing in considerable detail each of the stages of the discussion of this report, after telling us of the discussion which took place with the Minister of Trade of Commerce and the different officials, and giving all the reasons why the report had not been published for more than ten months, the minister now comes before us and seeks to leave the impression that the difficulty in publishing this second report, except by the procedure of mimeographing-which is a well-accepted procedure in business and in government-is the explanation, in spite of the lengthy statement already made.

speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend does not want to misquote or misrepresent what I said, but I am afraid that, quite unintentionally, he is doing that at the moment. speechtext:
Be made public. If my hon. friends on the opposite side wish to be technical, I can be technical too. I do not raise this point as a point of substance, but the act states it is to be made public, and does not state by whom.
The point I wish to emphasize is this. As to any allegation that the Minister of Justice has broken the law and is open to all the penalties that have been mentioned by the member for Winnipeg North, it relates to non-publication within fifteen days. As to the period of time the leader of the opposition is talking about, as I explained in my longer address upon this subject, that is not a

matter of law but a matter of propriety in respect of which, from the standpoint of the opposition, we may be open to criticism. Then there is the argument that once the section had been broken we should have published the report as soon as possible thereafter. The reasons which we gave for not publishing within that longer period of time, for not acting in a proper manner from a political rather than a legal standpoint, I presume are not concurred in by the members of the opposition. But so far as the breach of the act itself is concerned, I am sure even a layman would agree that the offence, if any, is complete when the fifteen-day period is up. It is complete, and it is at an end.
The matter of the publication of a report which is quite different from the report which was received is another matter, and I take it my hon. friend was not dealing with that.

This matter becomes worse every time the minister makes further remarks about it. I am quite sure the minister has not forgotten that I said, and others have said, that if the minister had explained that he was in Winnipeg, ill, and unable to be here immediately after his appointment, and that after his arrival there was an accumulation of work which made it impossible to comply with the provisions for publication,- I use the word "publication", because that is what it means, to make public-no one in the house would have done otherwise than to say that was a reasonable explanation which we could accept. No one would say that the failure to publish for a few days, or even a few weeks, should be regarded as a serious breach of the law, or a serious breach of the responsibility of the Minister of Justice and the members of the government who concurred in the procedure. But the minister himself has made it clear and beyond all question that his inability to deal with this matter quickly in the month of January had nothing in the world to do with the fact that this report was not made public until a short time ago, for more than ten months after it should have been made public. He has made it perfectly clear why publication did not take place. He has made it clear that publication did not take place because the Minister of Trade and Commerce first of all objected, did not agree with the findings of fact, and because after all these consultations there was general disagreement on the part of the government with the facts as they were found.
The Minister of Justice, making his explanations worse on every occasion, has now said that the act does not say by whom publication is to be made. The minister has explained that he received a copy of the report of the 45781-190
Supply-Justice
commissioner with an explanation as to the date on which publication should take place last January. He has made it plain on his own statement that it was on his initiative that the publication did not take place so far as the commission is concerned.
The act may not say specifically by whom the publication is to be arranged, but it most certainly leaves no doubt that the Minister of Justice has no authority to prevent publication, and that is what took place here. The commissioner appointed under the act was anxious to have publication, and said so, and it was the act of the Minister of Justice- for whom many hon. members have expressed real sympathy, in view of their feeling that he was placed under compelling pressure by another member of the cabinet, and that being a newcomer to office he was not able to resist that pressure at the time-it was the act of the Minister of Justice that prevented it. But that feeling of sympathy for the position of the minister is certainly removed when he says here first of all that the act does not say by whom publication shall be arranged, and suggests-and more than suggests in his remarks today-that the criticism that has been directed to the procedure is merely an attempt to damage his reputation, established over long years.
Even in his last remarks of a moment ago the minister said that this may be wrong from the standpoint of the opposition. May I impress upon every hon. member the effect of his words, that this of course may be wrong from the standpoint of the members of the opposition. By that he suggests, and more than suggests, that the standpoint is not wrong from the point of view of those who support the government. It is the only interpretation that can be put on these words. If that is the interpretation, then it makes the matter increasingly serious. Let no one in this chamber suggest that we are attaching too much seriousness to this procedure. On Thursday of last week a debate took place in the House of Lords in Great Britain, the first stage of the debate having been in the House of Commons, in regard to the conduct of Lord Pakenham, Minister of Civil Aviation in the United Kingdom. The circumstances there were in no way comparable with what has taken place here from the point of view of the seriousness of the course that was followed; nevertheless there is at least this similarity that can be noticed. A year ago last October there was a crash of a Dutch KLM passenger machine at Prestwick airport. As a result of that crash all the crew and passengers died. Under the statutory provisions covering such circumstances the Minister of Civil Aviation, Lord Pakenham, appointed a prominent barrister, Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Justice
McDonald, to conduct an inquiry into the circumstances. After the taking of extensive evidence, a report was made. Lord Pakenham kept the report for a period of five months. When the report was recently released he disagreed with the findings of fact contained in the report and refused to accept them. Anyone who questions the seriousness of a matter of that kind from the point of view of our parliamentary and administrative procedure should read the record of what took place in the House of Lords a week ago yesterday.
Lord Pakenham made his explanation in the House of Lords. He expressed regret that he had followed the course he did, but reiterated his non-agreement with the commission's findings of fact. In the discussion that followed it was pointed out that he had not heard the evidence; that he had not had the opportunity of exploring the details, and yet without that evidence and without those details he was taking it on himself to challenge the findings of fact made by a highly competent inquirer with the evidence actually before him. We find such great world figures in both constitutional and procedural law as Lord Reading and Lord Simon taking part in the debate.
In the opening discussion of Lord Pakenham's remarks, Lord Swinton dealt with what had occurred, and without covering it in detail I should like to read these words from the London Times of December 2, which gives an extensive report of the proceedings:
It was Inconceivable that the minister should' reject the findings of fact of a highly qualified tribunal unless he could satisfy parliament beyond all doubt that there was no proper evidence to support those findings. It was almost inconceivable that with a highly qualified lawyer sitting with an assessor such a situation would arise. Certainly no such situation arose here.
In the present case Lord Pakenham had, under the advice or direction of high authority, not retracted his previous statement but had retracted the method in which it was made. Most of their lordships would be greatly surprised at the form which Lord Pakenham's statement took today. If a minister could, in practice, cavalierly override the findings of fact of a highly competent quasijudicial tribunal in such a way as to render the whole procedure, in Mr. McDonald's words, "nugatory, if not indecent," no lawyer of repute would in future be willing to undertake the task.
There is a remarkable similarity in the situation here to what is referred to in these remarks.
In case there be any doubt as to what the attitude of these men was in regard to what had happened, Lord Swinton said that he did not think that after what Lord Pakenham had done and said, confidence in the
TMr. Drew.]
administration of that department could be maintained so long as Lord Pakenham continued as minister of that department.
Let no one suggest that when a minister, in regard to an extremely important matter, fails to carry out his obligation to parliament and to the public, there is anything in the nature of personal attack, or anything in the nature of an attempt to destroy a man, when the established practice is pointed out and the suggestion made that the proper course is for that minister no longer to be the head of that department. That, after all, was the view of great constitutional and procedural experts in England last week in connection with a minor breach of the responsibility of a minister to parliament and the public, as compared with the breach we have before us here.
As I said earlier, most hon. members had much sympathy for the position of the Minister of Justice on the basis of his earlier statements; and most hon. members I feel sure regretted greatly that the Minister of Justice should have found himself in a position in which his conduct was open to such severe criticism as it was in this case. When it was indicated that established practice and custom suggested that he should no longer continue as minister in that department, having regard to the explanation he had given, it was with the feeling that he had given an explanation which did indicate why he had failed to carry out his obligation. But that feeling cannot be quite the same after the minister's statement this morning, which he seeks to convey the impression that the failure to carry out the obligation was the result merely of practical difficulties, and that a criticism of this course was an attempt to destroy his reputation.
The Minister of Justice will recall that in the earlier discussion it was pointed out that the amendment he introduced to the Combines Investigation Act, which amendment has now been passed, gives to him a greater measure of responsibility for prosecution by making it possible under the act for the minister, in his capacity as attorney general, to institute proceedings under the Combines Investigation Act or the Criminal Code. It was pointed out that in view of the admitted breach of law by the Minister of Justice, with the consent and agreement of the government, he was placed in an invidious position in regard to the prosecution of other people under the same law or other laws of parliament. Already this morning section 164 of the Criminal Code has been read to the house;
I think it would be well to read it again:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to one year's imprisonment who, without

lawful excuse, disobeys any act of the parliament of Canada or of any legislature in Canada by wilfully doing any act which it forbids, or omitting to do any act which it requires to be done, unless some penalty or other mode of punishment is expressly provided by law.
I can find no provision which exempts any minister of the crown from the provisions of that act. Even assuming that many people may not regard this as serious, let them remember that others are compelled to obey these laws.
Section 573 of the Criminal Code provides:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to seven years' imprisonment who, in any case not hereinbefore provided for, conspires with any person to commit any indictable offence.
Well, there may be those who feel that it is inappropriate even to suggest that these sections should be read in connection with action of this kind on the part of a member of the government. But there certainly was an omission, and a deliberate omission, to do something called for by the act; and we are left in the position that from the government's point of view the only person who can advise the house whether this applies to the Minister of Justice is the Minister of Justice himself. Has the Minister of Justice considered whether in his capacity as attorney general he should launch a prosecution under either of these sections? The very asking of that question indicates the extraordinary position in which the minister has placed himself.
No matter what measure of seriousness or otherwise may be attached to this act, there was a plan; there was a holding back of the report by definite agreement and for a definite purpose. The Minister of Trade and Commerce did not agree with the findings of the report, and, so far as the explanations given earlier are concerned, it seems that the government collectively did not agree with those findings. So they took it upon themselves to become the tribunal, without having the opportunity to hear evidence; they took it upon themselves to make a decision in regard to a quasi-judicial finding which under the act could become the basis of subsequent procedure, and under circumstances similar to those in which Lord Pakenham made the decision which is under vigorous criticism in Great Britain today.
I am not suggesting that we should necessarily follow any governmental procedure other than that established here. But the practice in the matter of the responsibility of the government to parliament has evolved from traditions brought here from Westminster, and their attitude toward matters of
Supply-Justice
this kind is at least helpful to us in determining what others, under the same procedure, believe to be the duties of a government and the duties of ministers of the crown responsible for the fulfilment of obligations under any statutory provision.
One of the greatest authorities on constitutional law, Dicey, says this in the ninth edition of "The Law of the Constitution," at page 193:
With us every official, from the Prime Minister down to a constable or collector of taxes, is under the same responsibility for every act done without legal justification as any other citizen.
I do not think the position could be more clearly stated. The law was broken not because of pressure of time; the law was broken by a decision of the government concurred in by the Minister of Justice. No matter what the appropriate action would be on the part of any other member of the government, the fact is that the Minister of Justice is the minister charged with the legal affairs of this administration. In his capacity as attorney general he is responsible for the prosecution of individuals and corporations under the law as passed by parliament.
I can only conclude by expressing my regret that what was already bad was made infinitely worse by the spurious explanation given this morning by the Minister of Justice for what took place. The Minister of Justice, having taken the responsibility for breaking the law, and breaking it deliberately for over ten months, is not in a position to launch prosecutions under laws passed by this parliament without a feeling of injustice on the part of those who are prosecuted by him as Minister of Justice or as attorney general.
As has been said here before and on other occasions in this parliament, it is not open to hon. members to forget what minister it is who will be carrying out these responsibilities. I repeat that we are not dealing with this matter upon a personal basis in relation to any individual; we are dealing with the responsibility of parliament, and the fact that the government is responsible to parliament, and that if it fails in that responsibility it must take appropriate action to restore its position, otherwise the constitutional responsibility of the government to parliament will be impaired by the precedent so established.
As was said in the House of Lords last week in a much less serious case, no matter what our regard may be for the minister as an individual, no matter what our personal attitude may be as to the ultimate

consequence of what has been done, the failure of the minister to observe the law as passed by the parliament of Canada disentitles him to continue in this office, no matter what other office he may get; and confidence in the administration of this act and other acts cannot be restored while he is the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada.
That is the situation with which we are confronted. The explanation given this morning only adds to the concern that everyone has as to what else may have been done by those who still hold this point of view in regard to the responsibility of government to parliament. What has been done cannot be changed, but it is our duty to maintain public confidence in our system of government. It is the duty of parliament to assert its authority and to demand that the government respect its responsibility to parliament as a whole. Therefore the course that has been indicated is the course that should be followed in the interests of the preservation of our system of responsible government and the restoration of confidence in the minds of the public that, to use the words of Dicey, every official, from the Prime Minister down to the constable or collector of taxes, shall be under the same responsibility as any other citizen for every act done without legal justification.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not take more than two or three minutes to answer the long speech of the leader of the opposition, delivered in the solemn tones he has used, with his reference to great principles and so forth. With all that no one disagrees; but with the facts as they exist I think no one can disagree, not even the leader of opposition and the other members of the opposition.
The leader of the opposition closed his remarks by saying that what has been done cannot be changed. That is the kernel of this whole debate. What has been done cannot be changed, and what has been done was done inadvertently by pressure of time. The law requires that a certain thing be done within fifteen days. The report was not published within fifteen days because neither the minister nor any member of the government had been apprised of it. After the fifteen days had elapsed, what had not been done could not be changed.
The law does not say that if there is inability to comply with the requirements during that period, it shall be done as soon as possible afterwards. The law says that it shall be done within fifteen days and it was not done within fifteen days. That is

the situation in fact. The leader of the opposition says that there was no lawful justification or excuse or anything else; but there was the factual justification and excuse in that the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act says that it is now, in a different case, an impossibility to make publication in the way that has always been regarded as proper compliance with the statute. That is what had taken place before anyone's attention was called to the matter at all.
As the Minister of Justice said this morning, afterwards there was no possibility of complying with the express terms of the law, but there was the matter of propriety to be considered. Hon. members may form their own opinions whether the reasons given to justify the propriety of the delay after the fifteen days had gone by were or were not good reasons. That is something which has nothing to do with compliance with the statute. The statute had not been complied with, and could no longer be complied with. There remained the question of propriety as to what was the right thing to do afterwards.
Explanations have been given for the delay that occurred in choosing and fixing a time when publicity would be given to this report. The report contained suggestions that a line of conduct should be adopted which the government felt it was not proper to adopt under the circumstances, because we knew what had been the reasons for the conduct of those who are named as having been guilty of practices prohibited by the Combines Investigation Act.
That is the whole situation. The failure to make a report public is not a continuing offence as the leader of the opposition suggests. You cannot continue the offence. If a thing has to be done within a certain time, it has to be done within that time or it is not done within that time. After the time has expired there is no further possibility of going back behind its expiry and performing the act required. What has been done cannot toe changed; and it was not done, as the leader of the opposition suggested, by deliberate omission or by a plan for holding back the report. The question of publication did not arise at all before the fifteen days had expired.
The leader of the opposition said the law was broken not by pressure of time but by deliberate decision. That is entirely contrary to the fact. It was broken by pressure of time, and there was no deliberate decision not to publish within fifteen days, because the question had not arisen. Afterwards the law was not operative, because it could not be complied with, and it was a question, as

the Minister of Justice has said, of what it was proper to do after compliance with the statute had become impossible. The minister has explained why what he did then was considered by him and by his colleagues to be proper under the circumstances.

It seems to me that the longer this is carried on the worse it gets. I am surprised that the Minister of Justice reopened the question this morning at all. I shall try to deal briefly with some of the very simple facts about this case in relation to what has been said this morning. The Minister of Justice made a great play on the use of the words "publication" and "publish". Section 27 (5) of the act says nothing about publishing. It simply requires the report to be made public.
A few days ago I referred to the fact that the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act requires the Minister of Finance to lay on the table of the house on October 31, if parliament is then in session, the public accounts and the report of the Auditor General. The minister also sought this morning to rely on the absence of certain words in the section, an argument which I confess was startling to me. He said that section 27 (5) of the act says that the report shall be published within fifteen days after it is submitted to the minister, but the section does not say by whom. The section makes it perfectly clear it is the minister to whom the report is transmitted. The section also makes it clear that, if under certain circumstances the commissioner were to tell the minister that he did not feel it should be published, the minister still has the authority to override that recommendation and make the report public. In other words, the plain ordinary meaning of the language, which reasonable and ordinary people would take from it, is quite clear, namely, that it is the minister who must make the report public.
The minister threw out a question. Let me throw one to him. Who, does he think, is supposed to publish the report according to the section? Does he think it was Mr. McGregor? What would have happened if Mr. McGregor, when the report was not published by the minister within fifteen days, had taken it upon himself to publish it? That would have been the end of Mr. McGregor. The minister would have said: That is my responsibility.

That is right; it is very simple. Tell that to the minister. When we try to do that we are accused of being technical. The law clearly says the report shall be made public within fifteen days. That has been the whole argument all the way through, and sections 164 and 573 of the Criminal Code, which have been read this morning are equally simple, clear and direct.

It seems to me that is one of the most iniquitous features of this whole matter. We had a session of parliament last spring; we were here from January until the end of April. For all I know the report may have been printed during that period of time, as some of my friends say it was. We were here, but it was kept secret from us. Then the government went to the country. said that the Liberals had all the trump cards, but this card was kept secret from the people as a whole.

Surely the plain meaning of the law cannot be stretched in that way. This morning the Prime Minister objected to the solemn tones of the leader of the opposition and to his references to great principles. I do not think it becomes the Prime Minister to use that kind of language. What we are trying to do is to defend some things that are simple, basic, sacred, and fundamental to our democracy

that is, the maintenance of the law, and the rule of law, which all must obey.
It was also said this morning by -the leader of the opposition and taken up by the Prime Minister that what is done is done and cannot be changed. That was what the leader of the opposition said; and the Prime Minister replied: Well, that's it; it has been done and cannot be changed, so what are you talking about? As I understand the whole rule of law, when people have done things that cannot be changed we may admit they cannot be changed, but there is such a thing as punishment; there is judgment which is meted out to people because they have broken the law. It is not pleasant for us to suggest that, as the other Stuart lost his head, this one should do so as well; or to suggest that he should spend a year in jail; or that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister, who conspired with him in this matter, .should spend seven years in jail, as set out in the Criminal Code. We are thinking of him in terms of the office he holds. No; they reopen the matter even after it has been

closed. I may say I had my file in this connection here on my desk, and even I was not sure that I could summon enough nerve to bring up the matter again when we reached the item dealing with the Combines Investigation Act, in view of the general opinion that this session should end. But the minister has done it for us, and done it in what spirit? He has done it in the determination to show that though he has clearly broken the law, he simply says: That is nothing; it is just an obsession with the members of the opposition.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the issue is really crystal clear. Even yet I believe the Minister of Justice and the government should change their whole attitude and express to the house and the country some real measure of apology. If they do not, we have no alternative but to continue to refer to what happened to that other Stuart; to continue to refer to instances in British parliamentary practice of ministers who have resigned because of acts like this, and to continue to refer to sections 164 and 573 of the Criminal Code, which provide one year's imprisonment in the one case and seven years' imprisonment in the other for those who do this sort of thing. The country expects some one of these courses to be followed.

I shall not detain the committee long, Mr. Chairman, but it seems to me that what has happened this morning is easily the most extraordinary thing that has happened during the course of this whole discussion. As the last hon. member to speak has said, it is probable that if the minister had not taken the most unusual course he adopted this morning of introducing this subject on a point of privilege, this matter might have rested where it was, at any rate for a time. But what has the minister done? First of all he has made what I might call, though I do not want to use the word in an offensive way, a sentimental appeal, which I am sure affected all of us, just as the last speaker said. But what did he do after that? Certainly there was no sign of a guilty conscience, but if there had been any sign of repentance it seems to me there still would have been a disposition on the part of those on this side of the house who have been critical to go as far as they could with the minister.
But what did we get then? We got a hairsplitting, logic-chopping defence. I am not going into the details, but it was the kind of defence a lawyer would bring up in a criminal case if he had no defence on the merits. He would get down to some technical, narrow and, as I said, hair-splitting issue; and if ever there was hair-splitting it was in the two suggestions made by the minister. The first
Supply-Justice
was that once you got to the sixteenth day it did not matter any longer. Here I turn to the Prime Minister's words, that once you passed the fifteen-day period the law was not operative. Apparently he took that idea from the Minister of Justice, though the Prime Minister is perfectly competent to reach his own conclusions. That was an extraordinary thing for the Minister of Justice to say to us-in effect, that once you got to the sixteenth day it really did not matter what happened after that. Then, as I say, we had nothing but what I would call a narrow, police-court, technical defence, there being no defence on the merits.
Then we come to the extraordinary speech by the Prime Minister, which to me is far worse than what was said by the Minister of Justice. In fact to me it is by far the worst thing that has occurred in this debate, partly because it came from the Prime Minister and partly because it came from a great lawyer. He began by saying that this had been done "inadvertently". As I understand it, that means without quite knowing what you were doing, when you were off guard, or when you were not looking. That was not the case here. One afternoon the Minister of Justice spent at least two and a half hours explaining to us in great detail how it was anything but inadvertent. He gave us a great many reasons, as a matter of fact, why it was justified, explaining to us how it had been carefully considered. After all that we have the Prime Minister come along saying it was "inadvertent" and pooh-poohing the seriousness of it, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Then we had perhaps the most extraordinary remark of all by the Prime Minister -that after the fifteen days the law was not operative. In other words, as I said a moment ago, once you got to the sixteenth day it did not matter what you did in the intervening months-incidentally during the time parliament was sitting, and during the time of an election campaign. According to the Prime Minister, during all that period they were perfectly free to do what they liked, because on the sixteenth day they had broken the law and therefore nothing worse could happen. It has been suggested to me that this is exactly as though a man who was carrying a pistol in his hand said, "Well, I am breaking the law anyway; therefore it doesn't matter much what I do with this pistol."
I have just one thing to add. When I spoke before on this matter I said we were still in the position of having had no apology and no promise for the future. It seems to me this morning that was doubly and triply underlined and doubled and triply worsened by the fact that the Minister of Justice came

Supply-Justice
here and raised the question again, giving this entirely new reason, this entirely new line of argument, more or less as an afterthought. Worst of all we have the Prime Minister coming in, again with no apologies and no promise for the future, pooh-poohing the whole thing and saying this is just a funny idea we on this side have dreamed up. I cannot help but believe that the minister, with his legal experience, must have listened to those sections of the code with some interest. I only knew of them myself yesterday. Certainly they seem to tell a very simple story.
Again I say, as I said before, that I hope and believe the government has not heard the end of this yet from the people of the country. I believe what has happened this morning will make the people of the country wonder what sort of custodians of the law they have in the Minister of Justice, and in the Prime Minister who aids and abets the Minister of Justice in the most extraordinary line of conduct he has followed this morning.

I am not prepared to make any concessions. We came here this morning to discuss the estimates of the Minister of Justice, and, as a matter of privilege, he chose to make a further explanation of the unexplainable. He has raised the question, and has been supported in that by the Prime Minister. This is a most serious situation, and deserves continued debate. A remark was made which implied that, because something had happened, nothing could be done. I want to leave no suggestion that I think nothing should be done. I thought I had made a clear suggestion as to the first step, and that is that under our constitutional procedure the minister should resign, in order to restore confidence in his department. Unless the interruption is only for the purpose

of passing an item, and then returning to this debate, I regret very much that I cannot consent to any other procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not think the leader of the opposition would take that position. Last night I announced, and I mentioned it twice, that we would take up for some time this morning the estimates of the Department of Justice for the purpose of passing item 122, remission service, in order to accommodate my colleague, the Solicitor General. Then I announced we would take up national health and welfare. I do not want to lecture the leader of the opposition, but under the rules, the business of the house is decided by the government. At three o'clock this afternoon we will take up national health and welfare.

I rise to continue this discussion, sir. What a spectacle we have witnessed in this House of Commons this morning! This is the most astounding chapter in what has been undoubtedly one of the darkest incidents, if not the darkest, in Canadian parliamentary history.
The Minister of Justice must have been lying awake at night thinking about this subject, because this morning he came here having thought up one bright new idea. He put forward the trivial excuse that he could not do otherwise than break the law, after spending hours in this house in recent weeks trying to justify what he did. Now he has dreamed up this latest excuse, and he says: Oh, I could not have done otherwise than break the law, because I could not get the report printed in time.
The minister began with what may fairly be termed a maudlin appeal to sympathy. It is completely irrelevant. Then he grasped at straws. He said: We could not have the report published, because we could not print it. That is not an answer -that would appeal to the intelligence of a public school child. The statute says it is his duty to make it public, and a delay in printing is no excuse for a failure to comply with that -provision. What we have witnessed here, sir, in this last and most trivial of all his excuses, this grasping at straws on the part of the Minister of Justice, has been an incredibly inept and desperate attempt to palliate, in a belated and blundering brainstorm, a deliberate, calculated and callous breach of the law.
Whether his breach of the law was due to inexperience in obeying -the law, or to weakness and impotence in the face of the behests of a blustering dictator in the cabinet, or a reprehensible attempt to cozen the votes of unsuspecting Canadians at the polls on

June 27, the fact remains that the Minister of Justice, who should be the chief law enforcement officer of Canada, has become Canada's No. 1 lawbreaker.
The Prime Minister, sir, in the amazing statement which fell from his lips this morning, tore to shreds that fundamental principle of our democratic and parliamentary institutions, that all men, regardless of rank and quality, are equal before and under the law. No man, whether or not he is a minister of the crown, has any right to override the law. It binds him just as much as it binds the humblest citizen in any walk of life. The Prime Minister, along with the Minister of Justice, has torn that fundamental rule to shreds. Those who sit with him on the treasury benches, participating as they did with the Minister of Justice in this deliberate breach of the law, are equally guilty.
Then, sir, what is the responsibility of every member in this house? I ask hon. members opposite, who will return to their constituencies shortly: are they going to go home and say that they have been parties to upholding this government in its wilful, flagrant breach of the law?
Yes.

It is a tremendous responsibility for any Canadian to bear, most of all a Canadian who has been elected to parliament, and who has taken his oath to uphold the laws of this country.

DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE 252. Departmental administration, $794,605.

When the house rose last night the minister had made a statement on the new products which were introduced in this country. I am glad the minister made that statement, because among other things he pointed out that while these products had been discovered, yet they were not available to the public at the present time. It remains for another discovery to be made. In ways other than the way the minister cited this product will have to be produced in a synthetic form. I appreciate the fact that in his speech the minister pointed out that these products are not available to the public. We would not like to delude the public into thinking that these things are available and could be used in the form of treatment.
The statement made by the minister deserves a great deal of consideration, because
Supply-National Health and Welfare this is one of the most important discoveries made for years. In fact it may revolutionize the whole system of treatment in medicine. In making this statement I should like to pay tribute to Dr. Collip and to Dr. Browne of McGill university and Dr. Selye, those Canadians who have done so much research and have played their part in making this product available to the public.
We should view with pride the fact that Canadians have been in the forefront in scientific research and investigation, and especially in the investigation of this product that will bring so much relief to suffering humanity. Therefore I wish to pay tribute to a man like Dr. Collip, for instance, who has done so much work in endocrinology, and to the other doctors who were associated with him, especially those Canadians who have made this product possible, and to the other workers. It is a sample of co-operation between research workers both in Canada and in the United States.
As the minister pointed out, we should be very careful to indicate to the public that while these products have reached the first stage in research, before they can become available to the public further work must be done, and that work is making them available to the public in a synthetic form.

Mr. Chairman, I have nothing to add to the words which the hon. member for Lanark has so well spoken concerning the statement made last night by the minister, except to say that every Canadian must view with a thrill of pride the noble part played by Canadians in the research work which has led to discovery and development of these two new drugs, cortisone and ACTH.
Sir, my remarks on this first item are going to be intentionally brief. We are dealing here with the estimates of a department which this year call for an expenditure of $397 million, in round figures, representing an increase of more than $21 million over the estimates voted for the same department last year. On the health side the total estimates amount to something over $47 million, an increase of more than $5 million over last year's estimates. On the welfare side the estimates amount to $350 million in round figures, an increase of over $16 million, compared with the total of $334 million appropriated on the welfare side of the department last year. In case there are any who look upon these proposed expenditures on health as large, I should like to say briefly, sir, that there is abundance of irrefutable evidence that ill health is one of the greatest causes of national economic loss. Dr. J. G. Cunningham, Ontario provincial director of industrial hygiene, recently estimated that

Canadian industry loses $100 million a year by sick absenteeism. He also pointed out that in Ontario alone a cut of one-third in time loss through sickness and accidents would save industry in that province alone $35 million a year, and that Canadian doctors are accordingly campaigning for wider industrial medical services. He added: Besides the dollar saving, they know industry will come to be the biggest field in preventive health work.
Can we assume, sir, complacently that the nation's health is sound? Those who so assume must have been rather rudely jarred by a statement made by Mr. J. H. Ross of Calgary, acting chairman of the National Council of Physical Fitness, in Ottawa on September 22, when he is reported to have said that there is a likelihood that Canadians are not as physically fit now as they were on V-E day. That is a striking statement from a man who is the acting chairman of the National Council of Physical Fitness. Therefore I say, sir, in the face of indisputable evidence as to the very serious loss that ill-health creates each year, no one will begrudge sound expenditures on the national health. All will wish, however, to see the utmost benefit from the taxpayer's dollar so spent.
But, sir, I do not think this committee can be satisfied with the progress that is being made in the field of health under the present administration. Had these estimates come up at an earlier stage of the session, I should have welcomed the opportunity to develop this theme more fully. But on this matter of delay in proceeding with a program of national health insurance I must perforce be brief. I recall, sir, what the Liberal party itself said in its promising mood, that mood in which it can be quite clear in its statements. When in such a mood it wrote into its platform at its convention in this city in 1948 these words:
The program-
That is to say, its national program of social security-
-will include-
And note the words that follow-
-health insurance covering medical, dental, surgical and hospital health services on a contributory basis.
I say, sir, these words are clear. There could not be anything clearer than that statement. In its promising moods that party is clear; but what about its moods of performance? Well, sir, there is anything but clarity in what we find by way of performance. On a number of occasions this house has tried to smoke out the present minister and the government on the subject of performing its promises to give this nation a national contributory system of health insurance, which 
will provide those benefits that were promised in the passage that I have just quoted from the national Liberal platform. We do not find a clear statement coming from the minister on the subject; we do not find performance, but lacking that on the ministerial level we do find something more encouraging on the official level.
I have before me a press dispatch of September 14, reporting a statement made by Dr. F. W. Jackson, director of insurance studies in this department, in his address to the Ontario Medical Association, District No. 5, at Streetsville that night. The press dispatch attributes to Dr. Jackson this statement:
A complete health service, including hospital and medical care insurance operated and organized by the provinces for the Canadian people, was predicted by Dr. F. W. Jackson.
Dr. Jackson said the evident demand for health insurance by the public and the acceptance of this fact by the major political parties would bring such a scheme into being.
"Our objective must be to see that everything medical science has to offer for promotion of health, prevention of diseases and cures of illnesses will be available to every citizen of Canada, no matter where he lives or what his economic status may be," said Dr. Jackson.
Now, sir, it is perfectly clear from statements which have emanated from responsible medical sources that the medical profession of this country is studying health insurance. At the same time that profession has set its face, as I hope we all have, against anything savouring of state medicine. For instance, one reads this report on the convention of the Canadian Medical Association at its meeting in Saskatoon on June 18:
The 13,000 doctors in Canada today are probably more concerned about health insurance than they are with any other facet of their profession.
Health insurance-how it is and how it might be operated in Canada and the forms it takes in other parts of the British commonwealth-overshadowed any other feature of the five-day Canadian Medical Association convention, which wound up here yesterday. Technological advances, usually the centre of interest, took second place . . .
The General Council held lengthy closed conferences on the subject and issued a report giving the association's official stand. It said the C.M.A. proposed to adopt "all means within its power to further the development and extension of prepaid medical care plans in Canada." But a national compulsory program of health insurance was described by Dr. Magner in an address as abhorrent to the medical profession.
On this same subject Dr. W. E. Gallie, former dean of medicine at the university of Toronto-
