Sir, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been asked repeatedly for a clear statement as to what the government are going to do, and do now, to fulfil their promise that they would introduce a national contributory health insurance plan. We do not want any more of those generalities, those evasions, which we have been given in the past. We want a clear statement, and we want an assurance of action.
I wish to make good my promise to be brief in these remarks on the first item. May I offer one or two suggestions to the minister as to how we might proceed more expeditiously, and, I suggest, more efficiently, in the discussion of the estimates. We have had considerable discussion on several occasions recently concerning reports and the giving of information. I think it is a deplorable fact that we must spend time in the committee of supply on these estimates trying to draw out information that ought to be available to hon. members long before they reach this stage of debate or this final stage of the session. If we are to do our duty in respect of these estimates it will be necessary to ask for certain information, but I want to place the responsibility for our having to ask for that information at this stage and in this committee squarely upon the shoulders of the minister, because the report of his department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1949, has not been made available to hon. members. The last report from that department is the one for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1948, twenty months ago. The last fiscal year ended eight months ago. How much time is required to get out and to circulate these annual reports?
Section 11 of the Department of National Health and Welfare Act, chapter 22 of the statutes for 1944-45, states:
The minister shall submit annually a report to parliament in such form as may be prescribed by the governor in council.
That is to be done annually. Apparently the minister's idea is that he will submit the report to the next session of parliament, at which time it will be stale. I put the responsibility squarely upon the minister for failing to make available to members of parliament the report of his department for the fiscal year which closed eight months ago. We do not want any more excuses about the difficulty of having the printing done. Surely eight months is ample time to print all the reports of government departments. If it becomes impossible for the government, working at its lethargic pace, to have these reports printed, then certainly their minimum duty is to provide reports in another form which would not take as much time. There is a great deal of information an annual report contains which should be available to all members. Because of the default of the government in carrying out a plain duty, that report is not available.
The other suggestion, looking to the saving of time at this stage of the session and in this committee of supply, has reference to reports of expenditures over the year. For the last six sessions I have raised this question with the present minister, pointing out to him that before the estimates of his department pass we wish to know item by item, and in the aggregate, the expenditure of the department in the last year. We are given in the volume of estimates the appropriations for the year. This is a young department, and one can understand its difficulty in coming close in its estimates. We hope the department has now developed to the point where the estimates will be much closer and more accurate than they have been in times past.
To save time, I am asking the minister if he will give this committee of supply, before we leave the first item, the actual expenditures in the last fiscal year, item by item, so that it will not be necessary for us to rise on every item and ask the minister what the expenditures on that item have been in the last fiscal year.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I intend to be brief. I, too, join with other hon. members in saying how pleased I was last evening to hear the minister's statement that some important discoveries had been made for the relief of arthritis, one of the great scourges in our country. I am hoping that

Supply-National Health and Welfare that discovery will fan out to other incurable diseases of a similar nature which have caused untold misery and suffering among so many of our people for long periods of time.
This is a very important department. Like the hon. member for Eglinton, I too hope that during the lifetime of this parliament we may have a comprehensive plan of health benefits placed before the house for its consideration. Unlike the hon. member, I do not believe that we should fight shy of consideration of a completely socialized medical and health plan. I noticed his reference to Great Britain and New Zealand. Well, we shall know more of the working out of those plans in the course of the next few years. Although I did not bring it with me, I remember reading a statement made to a meeting of the medical profession in my own province by a well-known British doctor that was far from critical of all details of the plan in effect in Great Britain. I have followed closely the reaction of medical men and of the people generally in Great Britain. One point we should consider is that no matter what government may be in power in Great Britain after the next election, the popularity of the health plan inaugurated by the Labour government will be continued. The opposition party is pledged to expand rather than contract it. I have placed before the house on previous occasions evidence to show that doctors who were opposed to it when it was established are now speaking favourably of the plan.
I do not want to read any of these opinions at this stage of the session, because I do not think they would be of material interest in connection with the problem we are now discussing. What I really rose to say was this. We may talk about health plans all we wish; we may talk about advances in medical science; we may talk about the benefits conferred by a national health plan of medical aid and hospitalization, but after all, we must build up the health of the people right from the ground. In other words, we have to start by seeing that the children of this country are healthy and well fed. I have very high regard for the minister's interest in these particular matters. Interested as his department is in nutrition, I think the minister should place every pressure upon his colleagues in the cabinet and upon the various departments of government concerned so that there will be work for those who need work, help for those who cannot work; so that families will not be faced with undernourishment, which creates the greatest and most permanent difficulty in the field of health.
I have in my hand a clipping which I took from the Ottawa Citizen of the night before last. It is dated from Halifax, Nova Scotia, and reads:
Increasing numbers of undernourished children attending Halifax schools is causing city health and welfare officials serious concern, a civic official said yesterday.
Doctor R. G. Rice, director of child health for city schools, told the public health and welfare committee the situation was a result of poor economic conditions in many Halifax homes. The high price of milk had caused it to disappear from many tables in the city.
Breakfast was the poorest meal of the day for many children, he added. ''A surprising number of children come to school with no breakfast at all; others have only tea and toast."
Yesterday we were discussing the international children's relief fund. I warmly supported our contribution to that fund, but I said that while I believed in relieving distress among people beyond our borders, I thought that charity should begin at home and that we should see that something was done for the undernourished children of this country. The statistics show that because of the high cost of living, which has been made greater by increased rents, thousands of children are undernourished.
I do hope that a national health plan will not be delayed on the excuse that we have not sufficient hospitals, that we have not sufficient hospital beds, that we have not sufficient doctors or sufficient nurses. If we wait for all these we shall not put into effect the kind of national health plan that we need. I do not think we should wait until we have hospital accommodation and facilities. Indeed I think public opinion will support the building of hospitals and medical institutions and other facilities as they become more aware of the fact that they are needed. Once we begin to root out the people who need treatment in these institutions, public opinion will become aware of the necessity of providing greater appropriations for the hospital and medical facilities that we need.
I ask the minister not to delay this. Let us go forward. Let this parliament and this government fulfil the promise made in the Liberal manifesto which the hon. member for Eglinton read, so that we may have a national health plan. I should like to see that national health plan a part of a general social security plan. I am not sold on the piecemeal idea of saying: Let us have national health insurance on a contributory basis, or: Let us have old age pensions on a contributory basis. What we need is a comprehensive social security plan on a contributory basis providing for unemployment relief, family allowances, old age pensions, health and the other social security measures that we need.

The world is moving fast in that direction. I am not afraid to advocate what is sometimes called the welfare state. I know that that term has been used as a term of ridicule by the opponents of measures of this kind, but if we go back into the history of free peoples for the last fifty or one hundred years we find that as people became more secure in their jobs, with old age pensions at the end, with better health and all the rest of it, the efficiency of the individual and of industry has increased, apart altogether from the improvement in the field of health and the greater happiness of mankind. This is the main thing for governments to consider.
I know it is sometimes said that these social security measures would give the people a great deal of leisure, that they would not have to think so much of the future and it would therefore undermine initiative, and all the rest of it. Looking back over history I see that those within the British commonwealth, many men and women, who contributed to our culture, many of the great poets, the great writers, the great painters, the great thinkers and the great political leaders, were not faced with economic insecurity. Very largely they were people who were economically secure, both in their productive years and at the end of their lives. Consequently I think that this is one problem this parliament must face; it is one obligation that must be assumed, to see to it that we have a national security plan, and as part of that plan I would give priority at the present time to an all-inclusive national health plan.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that in the field of health the federal government is doing all that can be done within the terms of the constitution. While health grants are made by the federal government to the provinces, many of the provinces have not the funds with which to take advantage of them, because they are contingent upon the provinces being in position to put up dollar for dollar with the federal government. I am glad the government has seen fit to take steps to amend our constitution because I have been of the opinion for a long time that those in authority provincially, and who have had the responsibility for social security measures without having the funds to provide them, were very shortsighted in wanting to maintain their jurisdiction to take care of the poor, the maimed and the afflicted, without being in a position to do very much about it. In the time that the health program mapped out by the federal government has been in operation, it has done very little to take care of the people actually affected.
Supply-National Health and Welfare
So far most of the grants have been utilized in the expansion of hospital bed space. So far as my own province is concerned, and I think it is true of the whole of Canada, there is not much use building hospitals, training nurses and providing specialists if the people who are afflicted are unable to pay for these services. There is not much use improving, as they did, the Halifax general hospital and at the same time fixing the rates at $6 to $12 a day thereby making it impossible for ninety per cent of the people of that province to get into the hospital. That is something that will have to be corrected. I am reliably informed that some of the provinces have suggested to the minister that the federal government is placing them on the spot by offering certain amounts of money to be matched by the provinces for the purpose of expanding this program. That is positive proof we are not going to make the progress in national health we desire to make until such time as constitutional arrangements are made which will enable the federal government to put into operation the measures for which appropriations are made.
Last night I listened with a great deal of attention to the statement of the minister as to the development of new drugs, and I also read very carefully his statement in the press. I believe that the minister, as a layman in the field of medicine, feels that great progress is going to be made, particularly in the treatment of arthritis. In the section of the country from which I come, anyone who has worked for any length of time in heavy industry, particularly in the mines, is afflicted with some form of arthritis, rheumatism or allied diseases. Changing temperatures, heavy work and injuries from time to time bring that about. I know that the mining section of the north is affected in the same way.
I am sceptical whether the development of new drugs under the present plan will bring much relief to those who suffer from that affliction. In the great majority of cases those who suffer are unable to pay for specialized treatment. Drugs of that description are going to be expensive, and if they are going to be handed over to the drug manufacturers of North America, one of the biggest combines on the continent, after their development by the expenditure of public funds for research, very little of these drugs is going to trickle through to those who cannot afford them. The same thing applies to streptomycin and penicillin. They are expensive drugs, and in the great majority of cases those who need them most, and cannot pay for them, do not receive them. While we are taking the initial steps in the development of the two new drugs mentioned by the minister, with all their potentialities

Supply-National Health and Welfare in the field of medicine, I hope the government will also see that the formulas for these drugs are kept as the property of the Canadian government until such time as a price can be arranged to fit the incomes of people who may be in need of that particular form of treatment. There is no use developing them unless they are going to be made available to the people who suffer. I know that with all the talk you hear about developments in the field of medicine-

I will say without fear of contradiction that medical services today in that particular part of the country were never at such a low level as they are at the present time.

Supply-National Health and Welfare my presence here if I did not bring before the minister, the house and the government at this time a problem which to me is a tragic and sordid picture, in fact appalling.
I refer to a band of approximately 320 Indians who are found in the district west, northwest and southwest of Rocky Mountain House in the province of Alberta. It includes approximately 120 Sunchild Cree Indians and approximately twenty Chippewa Indians, all of whom are treaty Indians, and a further band of approximately 200 Indians of the Chippewa tribe who have not accepted treaty. In what I am going to say this afternoon I want to make it perfectly clear that my principal purpose in speaking is to bring a problem before the minister rather than to level charges at the minister or at the government because of things which have not been done.
Speaking only recently in the United States the Minister of National Health and Welfare made one or two very significant observations which are closely related to this problem.
The minister always tries to make significant observations.
That is what Vishinsky does.
The minister does not always succeed.

In one case the minister said:
We are determined to keep abreast of the advances of medical science and to be impatient and intolerant of anything that debars our people from the best of health care.
The Indians are "our people". I want to emphasize that. Secondly the minister said:
In our democracies any neglect of the citizen's right to health opportunity dishonours the concept on which our countries were founded-that we should organize society for the good of all.
These Indians would be included in the word "all". Thirdly the minister said that in surveys which had been made recently his department found some health statistics that gave little cause for pride. Unfortunately I am going to have to say later, when referring to certain statistics, that there is little cause for pride in the information which I will bring forward.
Finally, and this is most significant in the light of what I am going to say later, the minister made an interesting statement when speaking to the American Public Health Association on October 25. I am quoting from the Journal for October 26, and since part of these words are in quotation marks I presume they are designed to represent exactly what he said. This was the statement:
Canada ... is determined not to permit "lack of money to lead to neglect of health."
That neglect of health is not tied up to any specific group of people; I would rather look upon it as being all-embracing. In

I realize that the 200 could go quite some distance toward having their problems solved were they prepared to accept the treaty, but there are a couple of very significant reasons why they have failed to do so, and I am going to have to mention those reasons a little later because they are tied in with this question of health.
It would alarm hon. members, I am sure, if I were to tell them that one-half the Indian children in that area never reach the age of sixteen. In the second place, it is asserted by reliable authorities that one-half the Indian babies born there are buried almost before they see the light of day. When the mobile clinic was in Rocky Mountain House a few months ago some of those Indians presented themselves for X-ray. Of those who presented themselves, thirty per cent had tuberculosis, either active or inactive. The doctors, who are very close to this problem, estimate that fifty per cent of all the Indians in that area have tuberculosis, either active or inactive. I have before me something that will be rather interesting, eight or ten admission reports relating to cases of Indians taken to the Charles Camsell Indian hospital in Edmonton. Each report is signed, and the ages of the Indians range from five years to thirty-four years.
I am not going into great detail but here, for example, is the card of a youngster five years old. The diagnosis is: far advanced; has apparently been ill for one year and failing steadily; worse in the last few months. Prognosis: hopeless. Here is the card of a boy sixteen years of age: far advanced; apparently ill for months but going downhill rapidly in the last two or three months. Prognosis: practically hopeless. Here is the card of an eleven year old child, which states that as nearly as they can determine this condition commenced in 1946, yet the child entered hospital only this year. I could go through all these admission reports and present a most appalling picture.
I might add to what I have said already that the doctors advise me that of all the Indians in that area who presented themselves for military service during the war, not one was passed as physically fit. There are no statistics I can get hold of that could be considered as reasonably reliable with respect to venereal disease, but here again the doctors who are on the spot advise me that the number affected is liable to run over fifty per cent, basing this estimate upon those who have come to them for other reasons.

Is it any wonder that I call this a tragic situation? Let us not forget that these people are human beings. Let us not forget that they love life, too. Let us not forget that they feel pain, as we do. Above all let us never forget that these Indian mothers and fathers love their children, too. Apart from that, however, they are an absolute menace to the white population among whom they circulate freely.
I have already said that some further assistance could be given 200 of these Indians if they would accept the treaty; but I doubt ii any great advantage would accrue to them when I consider the conditions that exisl among the 120 who are already treaty Indians Even among those Indians the situation is appalling. These conditions, we know, resull from a number of things including impropei and inadequate housing which leads to pneumonia and other diseases. They have nc definite employment; and there is no plan oi properly executed enterprise with respect tc these treaty Indians, though we have officials who are presumed to be looking after theii interests. They have practically no educational opportunities; but above all else nc satisfactory steps have been taken to conduc' a comprehensive health survey in that area which to me is absolutely essential.

Tenders are being advertised almost at once, and we will proceed as quickly as we can. Presumably it will be spring before construction can be commenced.
The main hospitals under construction are the big hospital at Sioux Lookout, which we hope to open some time in the new year; the one at Moose Factory which fills a long-felt need in one of the most congested areas of our Indian population, and in which, unfortunately, the t.b. rate is quite high. This will form part of a series of hospitals for attacking t.b., which I think deserves some of the commendation which hon. members have seen fit to give to the departmental personnel.
Unfortunately the Coqualeetza hospital was burned, but we are still occupying part of it. We have a fine hospital at Nanaimo. The Charles Camsell hospital at Edmonton is a 350-bed hospital, and is one of the best t.b. hospitals in the country. Supplemented by the one at The Pas, and one at Brandon, as well as by others that are about to be opened, and nursing stations which have been opened all over the country, I believe the hospital situation will be taken care of. I will not say this represents a new departure, but at least it represents a new attitude on the part of the government towards this highly important matter.

I must say that it is not always possible to draw the line.

Among a very large number of people, including the officials of the minister's own department, there is a widespread belief-I believe it is a correct one-that a great deal of the tuberculosis and other diseases to which Indians are particularly subject, and many of the earlier deaths of infants, are due to dietary deficiencies. If these dietary deficiencies could be corrected a great deal of the health problem would be solved. What is being done by the medical services for the Indians from the dietary point of view? Are they supplying any of the vitamins to overcome the deficiencies? Are they supplying extra food with a view to improving health conditions, apart from just keeping these people alive?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend of course has touched one of the basic points. The answer to his questions is yes. Through our nutrition people we are making surveys. We have the advantage of surveys which are made by other groups. We use our medical personnel, nurses and doctors, and our own departmental literature through the schools and so on where they have access to Indians. They do not always have access to them but we use whatever agencies we can to bring home to the Indian the importance of good nutrition. Family allowances of course have been a great help in this particular. I can only say to my hon. friend that the very vital and basic point that he has emphasized is one that has been very much on our minds in the pursuit and the discharge of these duties.

I make one further suggestion to the minister as to how he can overcome these dietary deficiencies to quite a considerable extent. He should persuade the Indian affairs department to increase the amount of what is called welfare allowances to Indians who are destitute and Indians who are partially destitute and unable to make a decent living or provide themselves with proper food. If the allowance which has been $7.80 a month per person were increased to twice that amount it would improve affairs . considerably. If it were increased to anything like the dominion's portion of the old age pension payment the more extreme of these dietary deficiencies would be overcome. I am quite sure the minister could do more by urging on the government that this measure be taken than in any other way.

The Auditor General has drawn attention to certain matters which I think call for a statement from the minister. On pages three and four of his report the Auditor General refers to a situation which has arisen through the method used to verify the age of children. He lists 144,662 cases as at March 31 where payments have been made pending verification of the age. In paragraph nine on page four he points out that overpayments subject to recovery at the end of the year, which I presume means March 31, amounted to $429,394. He points out further:
Overpayments occur, as a rule, because (a) proof of birth is not established, or (b) children are not being maintained by the applicant.
I think the committee is familiar with the statement made by the deputy minister of welfare indicating that steps were being taken to recover some of these amounts, but in paragraph 10 the Auditor General proceeds to make some concrete recommendations in reference to safeguards when he says:
From birth to the age of 16, family allowance payments total $1,128. The extent of overpayments and the time lag between date of payment and receipt of data from the bureau of statistics make desirable the introduction of safeguards; for example, requiring (a) evidence of birth to accompany application, and (b) a parent to furnish annual declarations that the child is alive, is being maintained by the parent and, if of school age, is attending school.
I think those comments are worthy of the most serious consideration, and I ask the minister what steps he is proposing to take in the light of those recommendations?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend has called attention to a statement made when I was away and which otherwise would have been made under my name. That statement was made by the deputy minister on the welfare side on my instructions because I realized that while the press reports no doubt were intended to be helpful, actually they did not give a true picture of the situation. In order to put things in a proper perspective may I


say that in the last two years only $163 of overpayments have resulted through a lack of immediate birth verification. When you consider that in the last two years between $500 million and $600 million has been paid out by way of family allowances, and that there have been overpayments in the amount of only $163 for want of immediate birth verification, I think my hon. friend will find that the situation is one for which the administration of family allowances should be commended. I may say that the $163 was recovered. I think that statement ought to be underlined.
There were, on March 31 last, overpayments, in the amount stated by my hon. friend, of $429,394, out of gross disbursements made to date exceeding $1,100 million. Overpayments not yet recovered represent less than one-twentieth of one per cent of total family allowance payments.
Since the statement of the Auditor General came out, I have had an opportunity of examining the overpayment situation in those countries where family allowances prevail, and while I do not propose to give all the details today-it would take too long- my hon. friend will find that we not only compare very favourably but that our record is a record indeed in this respect.
The question really boils down to this. We have to make up our minds what we wish to accomplish with regard to birth tion as to birth verification, when family ance payment to be made as quickly as possible after birth? That was the intention of the house when the act was passed, and I think properly so.
In the case of the province of Quebec we were unable to get the same kind of collaboration as to birth verification, when family allowances came into being, as we got in the other provinces, and that fact accounts for the seemingly large proportion of overpayments in that province compared with other provinces. It was not because honesty is less prevalent there than elsewhere, but rather because it was not possible to obtain the same measure of early verification that we were able to get as a result of the co-operation given by other provincial governments.
As a matter of faot, a very small amount of the total overpayments are due to want of birth verifications. It is due to many other factors such as overpayments resulting from situations arising in respect of non-attendance at school, non-maintenance, the death of a child, non-residence, duplicate accounts, immigration regulations, children working for wages, and so on.

Therefore it is wrong to assume that the mere fact that birth verification does not immediately attend the registration for family allowance is the main circumstance which provokes this overpayment situation. We are anxious to give the payments to parents as quickly as possible at a time when they need them. If we had to wait until such time as the birth certificate came in, the family allowance payment would be delayed beyond measure, and our experience has shown that the trust which we place in the ordinary Canadian parent is more than justified. I do not think I need to say any more than that. We have to make up our minds whether we wish to provide family allowance payments as early as possible or wait until they are backed by a birth certificate. If the latter takes place, parents may not get the family allowances for several months, possibly longer. We feel the time to give the family allowance is as early as possible. Current verifications are now taking place as quickly as possible, and as I have indicated there have been overpayments in regard to new applications in the last two years only to the extent of $163 for want of immediate birth verification.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Let me finish my statement, and perhaps my hon. friend will agree that I have dealt with the matter pretty responsibly. In 1945 the government did make a certain proposition to the provinces, which was conditioned upon certain other actions by the provinces involving tax agreements and the like. That proposal inevitably was part of a whole pattern, a whole series of proposals.
Our means test in this country is as liberal as any other means test found in any part of the world. That is the first thing. No country has eliminated the means test. They have it in the United States; they have it in Australia; they have it in the United Kingdom; and they have it in New Zealand. Those are the facts. There are difficulties. I am not saying our situation is perfect; but until such time as we have a contributory system of old age pensions I say it is irresponsible to talk about the elimination of the means test.
To talk about liberalizing the means test is another matter. No one has a greater interest in this matter than I have, but I believe one
45781-192i
Supply-National Health and Welfare must put the whole subject before the country. We are spending now on federal account $100 million on old age pensions. The old age population of Canada represents a growing percentage of the total population. There are
625,000	people of the age of seventy in Canada today. Of that number 275,000 are in receipt of old age pensions. There are 4,200,000 children receiving the family allowance. Total family allowance payments are less than $300 million. If we were to leave the basic pension at the present level of $40 a month and eliminate the means test completely, without lowering the age, the cost would be $300 million. I ask the house to bear that figure in mind. To leave the old age pension at the basic rate of $40 per month and lower the age for women only to 65 would cost $391 million. To leave the pension at $40 a month and lower the age to 65 for men and women would cost $491 million. To put the pension at $50, lower the age and take away the means test would cost $614 million.
Those are the facts. I ask hon. members to consider them. No one can take away from my appreciation of the importance of our social welfare plans in the kind of economy we have in the western world; but having in mind the facts I have just stated, bearing in mind that we hope there will be extensions of other phases of social security at the right time and in the light of conditions that prevail, hon. members should ask themselves whether they think, in the absence of a contributory system of one sort or another- there being several kinds of contributory systems-it is possible to completely eliminate the means test. I say it has not been done anywhere. I say that the abolition of the means test must be associated with the adoption of the principle of contribution in some form, a matter which is receiving our fullest attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I intend to deal with only one aspect of this matter, Mr. Chairman, because I do not desire to make any extensive remarks in regard to what should be done. That is so for the simple reason that anything suggested cannot be done at this particular point, no matter how much we might wish it. At the moment we are dealing with items calling for expenditures based upon legislation already adopted. No matter how convincing any argument might be at this time it cannot change the basis upon which these items are put forward. It is within the power of the house, if the arguments presented should be so convincing, to strike out any item. It is not within the power of the house as a whole to increase an item, except on motion of the government. Therefore I wish to make it clear that my failure to enlarge upon what I think should be done arises only because
3020	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Health and Welfare personally I do not feel that a discussion can produce any practical results at the present moment, and that the appropriate time for such a discussion will be next session, when we have the broad program of legislation under consideration.
In making that statement I am not presuming to be critical of anyone who has expressed an opinion in regard to a subject which is of great concern and great importance to the people of Canada. The only reason I am rising to speak at the moment is that I do want to place on record the simple circumstances which relate to why as yet there has not been any effective provision for action by the dominion and provincial governments to deal with this subject on the basis of a broad, joint contributory plan. I am not quite sure why the minister introduced the fact that proposals had been put forward by the dominion government in 1945 embracing certain provisions of this kind; but since this does become a record I wish to make it quite clear that there is only one reason why consideration has not yet been given to a broad, contributory plan approved by both the dominion and the provinces. That is because the dominion government has firmly refused to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference since the last conference adjourned on motion of the dominion government on May 3, 1946. This may be constant repetition in the minds of some people, but obviously only by constant repetition can the truth be kept clearly before the people. Because of the fact that this has been raised by the minister I can only express my regret-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is not quite the truth.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is the exact truth; and I intend to keep that truth on record in this house. I want to express my regret that the dominion-provincial conference at which general problems of this kind can be discussed, as announced recently, will not take place until next fall. This means that on the very proposition put forward by the minister there can be no consideration until the session of 1951, on the basis of joint action by the different governments. I would point out that the conference that will be called is only being called because it is necessary, owing to the termination of the financial agreements that were signed, and which were not, incidentally, the financial arrangements before the conference of 1945-46.
That is all I propose to say, but I wish to make it quite clear, and the record cannot be challenged, that these joint plans can only result from the combined action of the dominion-provincial governments, in view of both the constitutional position and the administrative problems involved. It is a


matter of regret that the conference has not been convened to deal with that up to now, and the next conference will not be called until the autumn of the coming year. In keeping with the feeling of the committee, I shall be very brief. I know there are others who are of the same mind as I am in regard to this item of assistance to schools of social work. For that reason I am going to be brief.
A brief was submitted to the minister by the national committee of Canadian schools of social work on this item. I consider the contentions in the brief in support of increased grants for schools for social workers are unanswerable. I do hope that the minister will make the most strenuous efforts to increase those grants. They are needed by Canadian schools of social work to cover part of their administration expenses, and to provide student bursaries. The personnel situation in social work in Canada
Supply-National Health and Welfare is still very critical, and unless these schools receive federal assistance there is going to be a continuation of the crisis in the matter of personnel engaged in social work. The fact that the D.V.A. assistance is in process of being reduced as the number of student veterans who are attending the schools of social work graduate contributes to the critical situation that exists.
In line with the program that the national committee of these schools submitted to the minister it had been expected that grants in the neighbourhood of $130,000 would be available this year and $178,000 next year. For my part I commend this to the minister and urge him to give it active support.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot take the responsibility of delaying the committee. The chairman himself and the minister will have to do that. In my opinion this is one of the most important items that we have discussed and I propose to discuss it. Personally I should like to back up the remarks made by the hon. member from Cape Breton South. I consider this haste with the estimates scandalous and unrealistic. In my opinion, if these estimates are to be discussed as they should be discussed we should sit here until Wednesday night at the very least.
Having said that I shall say that I am deputed by a number of my colleagues to shorten this debate by saying on their behalf what I am about to say. Perhaps that will substitute one speech for four. I have been spoken to in that regard by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Yale, each of whom had expressed his intention to say a word or two.
I was glad to hear the minister say that he took second place to no one in a desire to promote social welfare. Here is his opportunity. Personally I think this grant should be increased. I myself have had some connection with welfare work. I realize, and the committee must realize, that there is a great dearth of social workers in this country. I remember a number of years ago, when the present Prime Minister was minister of justice, I asked how many trained psychiatrists there were in connection with the penitentiaries, and he said there was one such person, and that he was attached to Kingston penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I regard the work the hon. member is urging as highly important, and I can only say I regret it greatly if this measure were not continued in another year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I can see one advantage in having these estimates brought forward under pressure. The minister is prepared to commit himself earlier than he would otherwise.
I want the estimate not only continued, but increased. I said I had been connected with family welfare work in Saskatoon, and one of the disadvantages with which we found ourselves faced was a lack of trained personnel for social work. It was almost impossible to obtain properly trained and qualified workers.
Some people think that good intentions are all that are necessary for the social worker.
I know however that, in addition to a natural aptitude for his work, he must have training of a high degree. I am referring to training in psychology or psychiatry, and human relations. The demand for social workers is increasing, and I propose to give one or two reasons why. In the first place mental instability is decidedly on the increase. We find that the average age of occupants of prisons is becoming lower. We find that the number of divorce cases in almost all the provinces, and throughout the country, is becoming higher.
Then there is the matter of the government's social program to be considered. There are increased public services rendered by governments in connection with which trained social workers are necessary. Personnel will have to be supplied. There are a number of schools of social welfare, which are entitled to this grant as the hon. member for Eglinton has pointed out. These are connected with universities-I shall not read the list because I think that is hardly necessary.
The grant in 1946-47 was $100,000, while in the two following years it was $50,000. I was disappointed when this year's grant was only $50,000 because, as I said in my opening sentence, I think it should have been increased.
These grants have substantially increased enrolments in these social schools. Without that assistance I doubt if the enrolments would have increased, and many of the students would not have been able to take the course. The grant for 1949-50 of only $50,000, in spite of the representations which have been made to the Department of National Health and Welfare, is disappointing. I might have said that the fact the D.V.A. training


scheme is now completed has some bearing on this question, because a great many people who were prepared to go into social service work under that scheme find it is no longer available to them.
The estimates this year would seem to indicate that any increase of this $50,000 in the future is uncertain. I would urge upon the minister the necessity for increasing this amount. I do not know what the schools have applied for. I have not read their brief with care.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is $178,000 for the next
year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I say, as my last word in this connection, that bursaries are necessary. The average student going into this work would be better qualified if he had a B.A. degree, or an academic degree of some sort with which to begin his studies in social work. The temptation for those with degrees is to go right to work and earn a living at once. I have known of several cases of people with considerable aptitude who said, "I cannot afford it; I will have to go to work at once at the thing for which I have been trained." Had there been some inducement in the form of a bursary or a scholarship these people, with their leaning towards social work, might have been induced to take further studies. I think we would get a much better type of person by that method. Under present circumstances they are reluctant to spend more time in schools or universities. As a final word let me express the hope that the minister will see fit in future to increase this amount.

My suggestion is that the minister ought to give some assurance that these grants would be continued for a period of three or five years so that the responsible schools may be built to a point where the people in the communities involved may take advantage of them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

During the early days of the last great war the president of the Canadian Red Cross happened to be a friend of mine who lived in Regina, and who is now a member of the court of appeal of that province. We graduated in law together; and if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) were here I might suggest to him that I would like to join my friend of law student days on the august bench of my province. When he assumed office as president of the Red Cross and came to Ottawa there was not a single copy of the Geneva convention in this city. In a worthy effort the government had the splendid idea that, as part of the war effort, it should take care of the financial responsibilities of the Red Cross. I am not criticizing the government

of that time for this, because we all assumed we knew what the Geneva convention said. That action, of course, would have been entirely opposed to the whole principle on which the Red Cross was founded. That organization only operates in other countries in time of war because of the fact that it is not supported by the governments of any of the contending parties. Since that time they have continued to do that work, and to follow the settlements back into the northern parts of the western provinces. May I say a special word in appreciation of the services of the nurses who have gone out to those outpost hospitals and in many cases served three, four, five or ten years in them, far removed from the cities, and lacking many of the amenities of life. Yet they have given a service to the community where there was no doctor, and very often great hardship-travelling at night by dog-team or perhaps by sleigh, and acting so as to serve the community in which these outpost hospitals were situated. These nurses deserve a special word of tribute from members of the House of Commons, and it gives me pleasure to tender it. May I commend the hon. member for Mount Royal upon having brought this bill before the house. I am sure it will receive unanimous support.
