Mr. Chairman, last February I brought to the attention of the house a situation where certain collaborators of the nazis had been allowed to enter Canada. The hon. member for Kamloops says "alleged collaborators." I have proof positive that they were collaborators of the nazis. Owing to the dissolution of the last parliament I could not continue the case
Supply-Mines and Resources which I was building up against one of them, Jacques de Bernonville. Several men were involved and perhaps I might refresh the memory of hon. members by giving in brief the dossiers I have and which are based upon official information given to me in certain returns brought down to the house.
Jean Louis Hue, who lived in the region of Saint Gaudens in France, was looked upon as the local recruiting agent for the dreaded militia of Vichy. He tried to use his authority to compel his subordinates to follow the directives of Vichy and was himself a member of the militia to whom he delivered weapons. He was sentenced by a magistrate at Toulouse to five years' imprisonment and national degradation for life. Sentence was passed in September 1945.
Julien Labedan was a uniformed and armed member of the militia who took part in operations against the maquis of Haute Savoie and unhesitatingly followed the orders of Darlan. He was sentenced to death at Toulouse during January, 1945, for treason.
Georges Montel, a doctor and surgeon, was appointed first assistant to the mayor of Annecy by the Vichy government and was an impassioned speaker for the cause of that government. He is reputed to have urged that war be declared against Britain and the United States. In 1946 he was sentenced to hard labour for life by the court of Haute Savoie.
Andre Boussat, another doctor, was found guilty of dealings with the nazis and sentenced by the court at Agen in July, 1945, to penal servitude for life. He was a moving spirit as well as an ardent propagandist for the militia.
Michel Seigneur, still another doctor, was a strong Vichyite and a member of the militia. He attended the school for militia leaders where his file stated that he was an "excellent element from every standpoint; among the first of his year; perfectly in his place." In March, 1945, he was sentenced to death at Poitiers. These men are now here in Canada.
There is still another and very much worse case. I refer to de Bernonville who worked with the Germans in north Africa and became military commandant of the Lyons area. As I said before, amongst his duties there was the identification of British and other allied officers who had been dropped into France by parachute and were subsequently caught. He was accused of having caused the death of many Frenchmen. In February of this year I partially placed upon the record the sworn testimony of Maurice Nedey who had been tortured by de Bernonville, but my time

Supply-Mines and Resources expiied before I could complete the statement. I may say now that Nedey was sent to Buchenwald camp and most fortunately escaped from there. A member of the house in the previous session, the member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, who I believe was counsel for de Bernonville, took exception to the things I said and he answered me on February 24, 1949. I am not going to take the time of the house to answer him, but I can assure hon. members many of the statements he made were quite inaccurate. I can only point to his allegation that according to the French ambassador ninety per cent of the maquis were communists. He stated the French ambassador said that, which is certainly not the case. He mistranslated a telegram, and he was responsible for other misstatements which can be proven. In approaching all these charges he implied that I was necessarily a sympathizer with communists, or communism. I repeat now what I said very bluntly before, that the man who thus accuses me, or any other members of my group in the house, is either a liar or a knave, and in all probability both. He accused me of harbouring sentiments against French people because I opposed the entry of these collaborators into Canada. That also is not true because when the government of Canada placed French citizens on exactly the same basis as any other individuals coming to this country, we were amongst the first to welcome this move. Even more stupidly I have been accused of anti-Catholicism because I opposed the entry of these men to Canada. I think my record in the house and outside of it will prove that I have no intolerance of any group because of race or religious belief. Such a concept is anathema to me. I do not know the religion of these men. All I know is their political records, and it is solely on the political basis that I oppose them.
I should point out, however, that when de Bernonville was sentenced to death it was not, as the member for Charlevoix-Saguenay said, when there was an alleged reign of terror in Toulouse in 1944. He was sentenced to death in October, 1947, when the premier of France was Mr. Paul Ramadier, and the minister of justice was Mr. Andre Marie who, if he were in this House of Commons, would feel perfectly at home in the ranks of the Conservative party.
I am told that once again a board has been set up to consider the de Bernonville case. I do not know whether or not that is so, but I should like to produce certain other evidence I said I had. I am not going to read it all, but if the minister does not have

copies I shall be very happy to supply him with these statements. There is one given by Julien Lessaque which reads:
I, the undersigned, Lessaque, Julien, commandant at Givry (Saone et Loire) attest that my brother, Lessaque, Jean, twenty years of age, from Rosey, Saone et Loire, belonging to the Cruchand Maquis took part in the battle with his group on June 12, 1944, with the occupants of Givry. He was wounded and captured by the militia stationed at Cortiamble, a suburb of Givry, under the command of de Bernonville. He was questioned and tortured and while in prison at Chalon, he managed to send me word. This paper was sent to the commandant of Chalon and Saone and was never returned to me. On July 18, 1944, I learned that my brother had been shot by the Germans. I am sure that my brother had only as his object to fight the aggressor and to liberate the country. It is therefore de Bernonville who is entirely responsible for his arrest, tortures, and his death. I truly hand over this present attestation in order that it may be put on the file of this unworthy Frenchman.
It is signed at Givry on November 23, 1948. I shall only read one other. There are others if the minister wishes them. This one is written by one Madame Bonnet whom de Bernonville made a widow. It reads:
I, the undersigned, Vv. Bonnet, Maurice, declare under oath having been arrested on May 31, 1944, by a group of militia men who were at Chalon-sur-Saone under the order of commandant de Bernonville. After having been closely questioned at the hotel Moderne, I was taken to the prison of Chalon-sur-Saone. I admit that they were not looking for me but for my husband as being a member of the resistance and who had just escaped them. I was to be released on June 24, as my husband was arrested again on June 9 during a battle at Givry, Saone and Loire, together with militia men and a group of F F.I. of whom he was the leader.
Very severely wounded by seven shots during this battle and taken prisoner, he went through terrible tortures, namely, hanged by the feet regardless of his severe wounds, then turned over to the Germans who left him forty days in the Chalon prison without any care and shot him on July 18 with one of his men (Lessaque) who was arrested with him. I add that de Bernonville was perfectly aware of the tortures inflicted by his men on the French he ordered to arrest.
That is signed by Madame Bonnet at Chalon-sur-Saone on November 21, 1948. As I say, there are many other instances which I could give to the house. But now I want to point out that one, Jean Bonnel, a resident of Montreal, said that de Bernonville was one of the heroes of France and instead of sending him to his death we should kiss his feet. He added these words:
I will do everything to keep de Bernonville from being delivered to the present government of France, a government of cretins, assassins and bandits.
One who is now a member of the house and also mayor of Montreal, Camillien Houde, stated that the deportation of de Bernonville would be "an iniquity". He went on to say:
This crying injustice-we can call it this infamy -cannot pass in silence.

We have other amazing declarations such as that of the judge of the court who, according to newspaper reports, said that he would ask the authorities at Ottawa to grant de Bernonville asylum in Canada along with his family. I think I might add to these testimonies that of Pierre Laval who was shot as a traitor in France. I will translate this very roughly. It is signed by Pierre Laval at Vichy and dated the 6th of July, 1944. It is to the effect that de Bernonville was becoming energetic in the militia. He proved on numerous occasions his ability to maintain order in Haute Savoie and distinguished himself in the way he defeated the maauis in certain engagements, details of which I have already given to the house.
I do not think there is any argument at all for the presence of de Bernonville in Canada. I am informed that the government intends to press for his deportation, and I hope they will be successful in their endeavour. There is more to it than merely the matter of de Bernonville. There is also the matter of statements which were made last year by ministers of the crown when this whole most obnoxious business was first exposed. The then minister of mines and resources declared in public that these men had been screened, and that they were accepted as being proper applicants for entry into this country. He was seconded in his statements by the then acting prime minister, who is now the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Both of these gentlemen said these men had been screened. I challenge the accuracy of that statement because it was not true. If it was true then the screening was most incompetent. What was even worse and more unbelievable was the suggestion that these men had been screened by officials of the department, and that therefore these officials were responsible for their entry into Canada by consenting to their coming here. That was entirely untrue because the officials of the department had recommended that these men be deported, and the government overruled their recommendations and accepted them into Canada. The then acting prime minister went even further. He spoke of hasty trials. When any hon. gentleman is acting as prime minister of a country he has to be rather judicious in the remarks he makes about the courts of a friendly nation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has all the finesse of a bull in a china shop when it comes to diplomacy, and he made an extraordinary mistake when he said that these trials had been hasty. Very shortly afterwards he was called upon by the
Supply-Mines and Resources ambassador of France who, after consultation with the minister, issued a statement. The following is the statement issued by the French ambassador:
The ambassador pointed out that the persons in question, who have been condemned in absentia, were tried by French courts according to correct legal procedures and found guilty of major crimes. He further stressed that their concern for their honour should prompt these Frenchmen to go and appear before the courts of their country, where every opportunity of defending themselves would be given to them.
The acting prime minister, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, issued the following statement:
X have seen the communique of his excellency the ambassador of France. I am able to confirm that at no time since the end of hostilities has the French government presented any request for extradition to the Canadian government, nor would I wish to question the ambassador's assurance that the trials in absentia were conducted according to correct legal procedure.
Of course that puts a rather different complexion on it because, as has been pointed out, justice, as it was meted out in France, has been lenient. There were 160,000 cases of collaboration reported, not many when one considers the four years of occupation. Some 820,000 French citizens were deported by the nazis. Some 222,000 were killed during deportation, and 30,636 were shot in France by the invaders. So far as French justice is concerned, of the 160,000 cases there were only 5,500 death sentences, and only 791 carried out. I do not think there can be any aspersions cast on French justice in that regard.
The Prime Minister also said, as one might expect in the light of cabinet loyalty, that he agreed with the regularizing of the entry of these nazi collaborators, and he said:
I am satisfied with that. In my judgment that should be final.
"Final" only in the judgment of the Prime Minister, Mr. Chairman. There are certain questions which I wish to ask the Minister of Mines and Resources. The first one is whether he can tell me the composition of the tribunal which has been appointed to consider the case of de Bernonville. Following upon that, I should like to know if the minister has any information about the trail of Michel Seigneur at Limoges in France.
Mr. Chairman-
I wonder if I might have my questions answered first.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the government for the job it has done in the field of immigration since the end of the war. In 1946 we were the first overseas nation to establish a mass immigration program from the displaced
3036	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Resources persons camps. We were pioneers in that field. We were the first from the new world to extend our hand to those unfortunates who were then rotting in the camps. We organized teams consisting of immigration, labour, medical and security officers who travelled from camp to camp recruiting, examining and processing. We procured transportation for displaced persons when it was very difficult to obtain. Two years later we were followed by the United States. To date we have welcomed 90,000 immigrants to Canada, and the United States with her vast population and resources has only taken in 120,000. In the light of these figures I think we can be very proud, and we can give credit where credit is due.
I want to say a word about the man who carried the administrative burden, the director, Mr. A. L. Jolliffe, who will have retired before we return for another session. He has been a great public servant who has spent thirty-seven years in the department during which time he has carried a very heavy load. It has not been an easy department because it deals with human beings. Many times it was an adjunct of some other department, and the immigration policy was not too clear. He has been an excellent administrator with a very penetrating mind, and has helped to carry out this country's achievements and objectives as to immigration. Many of his problems have been human problems, and he has brought consideration and understanding to them. He dealt with them in a fine warm-hearted manner as an honest man would. I think all members of the house will wish him well indeed.
I am happy to call the attention of the house to another matter, the attitude of the government with respect to those who have ventured across the Atlantic on their own.
I think this house knows that in August of last year a movement was commenced across the Atlantic from Sweden to Halifax, first by a motor vessel called the Astrid, carrying 29 Estonians, which was followed by nine other small vessels bringing a total of 987 persons, of whom only twelve have been refused admission to Canada. Recently another attempt was made by the S.S. Victory, which is now in Cork, Ireland, carrying 372 passengers, who are being inspected and cleared there. These refugees were people running away from oppression. They came to our shores seeking freedom and opportunity, and we generously admitted them. They were modern Vikings who demonstrated their desire for freedom in a way most of us are incapable of. The cost of this movement was considerable; we had to feed, transport and maintain them, and the government 

spent almost $150,000. In admitting them the government has placed humanity above regulations, and I think it should be praised for so doing. Canada has need for such bold and enterprising people, and the department has done the country a great service.
The news that a Department of Citizenship and Immigration is being set up is most welcome. I think it is a proper recognition of the relationship that exists between citizenship and immigration, and of the long-term importance of immigration to this country. It is also, I hope, an indication of a larger and more vigorous immigration policy in future. I am heartened by the words of the right hon. Prime Minister on Friday, December 2, at page 2596 of Hansard, when he said:
There is a probability that there will be an increasing number of persons admitted as immigrants into this country to share with us the advantages and responsibilities of developing the resources of Canada.
At another point on the same page, he said:
It is my view that our experience in that respect has demonstrated that, while it was principally on humanitarian grounds that these people were admitted to our country, they will ultimately prove that the bread we cast upon the waters is returning to us.
So, after a generation of inaction with an immigration policy which was tantamount to a non-immigration policy; after a generation in which the once important department of immigration dwindled almost to extinction; after a generation in which almost as many people left Canada as came to Canada; it has been heartening to see a new tide of immigrants coming to our shores. Those of us, and our number is increasing, who believe that large-scale immigration is the lifeblood of a young, vigorous nation, are gratified that the government has admitted more people to Canada in the last four years than it did in the whole preceding 14 years.
The latest figures indicate that Canadians are now staying at home. The border has lost its lure. We might ask what has suddenly happened in Canada? I wish to give this house five potent reasons that have fired the imagination of young and old in this country; they are the main reasons why Canadians are staying at home today. I remind this house, first, of Chalk River, with its scientific research; Polymer, with its great engineering advances; the western oil fields, with their liquid gold; Labrador, Ungava and Quebec, with their iron ore; and the Northwest Territories, which is an empire all its own. Truly, the twentieth century belongs to Canada. Those are frontiers that have, as yet, been unscratched. The natural resources are almost limitless.

The need for people is still with us. This great war has swelled the post-war wave of immigrants, but there is still plenty of room for more. Those who came to us have become part of the Canadian mosaic. They have enriched our economy and our culture, contrary to all predictions. As I have already stated, they have remained here. Is it any wonder that we should want more of them? When we look about, we find that the sources of immigration are drying up. With the exception of the countries on the western fringe of Europe, Russia has closed the continental door in our face. No one goes in, and no one comes out.
In Britain, the traditional source of much of our immigration, we find her economy so depleted she has taken in great numbers of them, too. Faced with that situation, we must revise our standards considerably if we want to retain our present healthy level of immigration. If the flow is dwindling, we must open the sluice wider. We have recently heard the news that immigration this year is falling far short of our figures for last year. The figure for 1949 is one-fifth less than for 1948; I think that is a serious situation, because that is one import upon which we cannot afford to cut down. People have always been our most valuable import. Unfortunately, many countries have had to establish a form of export control on people, and that is one reason for our falling immigration figures.
There are several solutions to this problem. The first is to extend the degree of relationship which renders immigrants admissible to this country. This is badly needed. At present, the regulations authorize the entry of certain categories of relatives, extending as far as unmarried nephews and nieces under the age of 21 years. Yet, the fact is that in four years we have drained that valuable field and also of mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, nephews and nieces; they have nearly all been spoken for. There are still many who want to come to Canada, and who would make good and useful citizens, but who fall outside the present categories of relationship. I do not believe there is one member in this house who has not had at least one heart-breaking case brought to his attention, and has been told that nothing can be done.
I ask this house, by what stretch of the imagination is a nephew 25 years old less desirable as an immigrant than his younger brother of eighteen? He is still excluded, however. Why should we admit a niece, but not a cousin? Why may a single man come in, yet we exclude married couples. I believe these categories are unrealistic. They should be abolished. If they cannot be abolished
Supply-Mines and Resources immediately, they ought to be abolished progressively. We could abolish them by gradually expanding the right, first to married nephews and nieces over 21 years of age; then to cousins, and then to any degree of relationship.
I think the test of admissibility to this country must be twofold. First, is the immigrant a useful citizen; and second, is there someone in Canada who will accept responsibility for him, who will guarantee accommodation and maintenance until he becomes self-supporting. Then, providing they are in good health, physically and ideologically, they should be encouraged to come to Canada to build new lives here. A second solution is to attract settlers from countries which, in the past, have sent us many fine Canadians. We want settlers from the British isles; of course we do.
Scotchmen.

There are none better. Then, of course, we can look at Scandinavia, Holland and France. I was thinking particularly of Italy, a land which, to my personal knowledge, has supplied us with some of our best citizens. Today Italy is a great reservoir of manpower, yet the Department of Labour Year Book indicates we have only brought in 250 Italians since the end of the war. They were immigrant workers, such as terrazzo workers, and stonemasons. Italy is a country that has always been overcrowded, lacking resources. Her economy is reduced to a point where she must export people, if she wishes to achieve any kind of stability. This is a great opportunity for us, and we cannot afford to miss it.
Italian settlers have come to Canada since the turn of the century. They are sober, hardworking people who have made a worth-while contribution to this country. The Italian settler fits in any place. He is a farmer, artisan, merchant and worker. When he comes to Canada, he comes here to stay. Canada has never been his half-way house. He is a permanent acquisition, and a very good one indeed. Today there are thousands of skilled and unskilled prospective settlers in Italy, who seek nothing better than an opportunity of coming to Canada. We, in turn, need them as much as they need us. Our absorptive capacity in this country has not even been scratched.
I should like to see this government mount a full scale immigration scheme, designed to draw us the best type of settlers from Italy and other free European countries. Our immigration service in Europe is now functioning, and functioning very well. I think they can handle a much larger flow than is at present passing through their office. We have helped a great deal to reduce the dis-

Supply-Mines and Resources placed persons population in Europe. Now I think we should turn to that portion of Europe's people who are not displaced persons and give them an opportunity to qualify for entry into Canada. We can do that best by expanding the classes of people who are admissible and by vigorously going after the very best type of immigrant.
I think it is highly significant that in our history periods of national prosperity and high immigration have usually coincided. I am not trying to propound the theory that prosperity causes immigration or vice versa, but I do believe that immigration and prosperity stimulate each other. A glance at the last four years would affirm it, and a look at our past history would reaffirm it. Our postwar immigrants have brought to this country brains and skills. They have founded scores of industries and have given employment to thousands. If we are to continue to grow in this country, if our national income is to continue to increase, if our prosperity is to last, we must have more people; we must have more customers and we must have more consumers and we must have a larger internal market. I plead again with the government and with the department to continue to stimulate immigration in this country. It is my firm belief that we must have more Canadians. In order to have more Canadians we must have more immigrants.
The minister has not answered my questions yet.

speakeroldname: Hon. Colin Gibson (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
The question the hon. member asked was first of all about the composition of the board that will consider the de Bernon-ville case. The board is arranged for. It consists of members of the department. It is not customary to give their names, as we do not want to have their names announced until the hearing actually takes place. Counsel has been appointed and the board hearing will be started as soon as the counsel is ready to proceed with the case.
My hon. friend also asked whether we had particulars of the trial of Michel Seigneur.
I would say that details of that kind do not come to my department; they go to the Department of Justice where any screening is arranged for, but we do not ourselves have the particulars of those files.

Can the
minister tell me where we can get the information contained in the sessional paper I have here, 61-H. I presume this did not come entirely from his department but from other departments as well.
[Mr. Croll.l
That was before I was in the department. I understand that was an order for return, and papers for that are supplied by all departments.

The reason I ask is that I have information that Seigneur was accused and condemned for having been an inspector general of the Wafifen S.S. I should like to remind the minister of this. In the last parliament seventy-nine days elapsed before this order for return, 61-H, came down. Seventy-nine days elapsed and I got it the day before the house dissolved. The government has beaten that record now. Since the notice of my question and the order for return was passed on de Bernonville over eighty days have elapsed and I do not have the information I should like to have. Nevertheless I was given certain information, certain transcriptions of evidence of the courts in France about these individuals. I have the transcript of the court of appeal about Seigneur. What I should like to know from the minister is whether the record of the trial at Limoges is in the possession of the department.

I do not know anything about it. The question has not been raised with me since I have been in the department. I have not looked into it. I do not know anything about the papers. If the government has any they are not in my department.

This is a serious matter. Here are men whom I accuse of being nazi collaborators. The minister knew I was going to bring up this matter. I would have thought that he would have made himself fully conversant with it, and would correct me if I am wrong or agree with me if I am right. I cannot find out this information about Seigneur at the moment. Therefore I pass on the information which I have here. I say that this man, whose entry into Canada has perhaps by now been legalized, was sentenced to death for being an inspector general of the Waffen S.S. I am talking about Seigneur now. All these men came into Canada on false passports, on forged passports. I should like to know what sort of security existed to allow them to come here when obviously they could have had no background but names which were assumed. Were they smuggled in?

Mr. Chairman, the cases that have been referred to were considered some time ago, before I was in the department. I understand that they were carefully screened at that time and the decision was made that they would be permitted to remain in this country. Since

then I have not heard from the hon. member that he had any further evidence that he wished to have considered, and certainly since I have been in the department I have not even looked at their files because the matter had not come up.

I am not
quoting the evidence now. I want to know how these men with false passports were screened. How could they be screened? The minister must know because evidence has been read into the record that his department officials and security officials recommended against their staying in Canada. He knows that. If any decision was made it was purely a political one, I assume at cabinet level. The minister ought to know something about that. While I am not accusing him the government must assume the responsibility. How were these men cleared by security if they had false passports?

Mr. Chairman, the fact that a person had a false passport does not conclusively prove that he is not a desirable person to enter this country. For example, people have escaped from other countries and come here and landed without any passport at all. They have had to be examined and screened to find out what their background was. If they were approved, they were allowed to stay. If they were not approved they were of course deported.
By whom?

Department officials and security officials recommended that they be sent back. They came into this country on false passports. We have been told that they were screened. How could they be screened? Yet I am told they were screened. They came in here with false passports, under false names. They could have no background at all. What sort of security is there? I know that there is security, and I have no objection to it. I think it is competent, but now I am told that these men were screened. I say they could not have been. Will the minister please be a little more specific and tell me how people with false passports and with false names could be screened. I want to know how that is done.

Mr. Chairman, the screening is done through the Department of Justice. We send to the Department of Justice any cases on which we require information. They have methods of securing reports on the individuals. If they are not satisfied and they do not give a clearance the individual is deported. If they are able to
Supply-Mines and Resources satisfy themselves and give a security clearance, then we are at liberty to admit them into this country.

These men were screened by officials of the Department of Justice and they recommended against their entry into this country. A section of the immigration law says-I have not the exact quotation here-that they should not be allowed into Canada because they are not of good character. What was the reason for the decision to permit them to stay here? Were there extenuating circumstances? The government knows that they had been accused and convicted in France of certain crimes against our allies. What circumstances prompted the government to permit these men to stay here, knowing that they had come on false passports, knowing that they had deported seven Jewish people for exactly the same reason? What was the distinction between the seven Jews and these collaborators?

I understand the reason the Prime Minister gave when this matter was up in the house before was that all the circumstances had been considered, and thoroughly considered. That is, they had decided that some of the men who had been able to satisfy the authorities would be permitted to remain in this country, and those who had not would be deported.

It is only right that we should know the circumstances, so that the names of these men can be cleared if they are not guilty. I have certain facts here which are damning. These are extracts from the trials appearing in sessional paper 61-H. The minister says there are extenuating circumstances, that there is something about the character of these men which I do not know, and which permits them to stay here. What were those circumstances, which were so important that they could override the provisions of the Immigration Act itself?

I cannot give the hon. member the information we have on confidential files. I can only say that the government at the time went over the material and decided that it would be justified in admitting certain ones and not admitting the others.

All I am
saying is that the minister has information which may redound to the credit of these nazi collaborators. In fairness to them, even allowing for any confidential files, he should make it public. I have put on record the case against them. The minister says he has

Supply-Mines and Resources confidential information in their favour. I ask, in fairness to them: Why not present that evidence?
Carried.
I would like to have an answer.
Just a word on this: I do not know the de Bernonvilles-
I know what this silence means.
Oh, oh.

I notice great laughter over here to my immediate right over my mispronunciation of the French name. I am quite sure the honourable member-and I emphasize the word "honourable"-would not respect me much if occasionally I were to laugh at his English, something which I never have done in this House of Commons.
My hon. friend is mistaken. I did not laugh. He is absolutely out of order.
Then I accept what you say, and I was quite wrong-as I will accept the word of any other hon. member, particularly the minister. But I wish the minister to tell me this-
I would never do that.

Doctor, I have done everything I can. I wish to ask this: The hon. member for Winnipeg North tells this House of Commons that certain people were convicted of crimes in France against the allies and came to this country fraudulently -and that is the only word one can use. It was thoroughly fraudulent. Now someone in the government service, as he has said, against the advice of departmental officials has decided that these people convicted even of murder, if I heard him correctly, and I think I did-
de Bernon-ville; the others are not accused of that.
In any event, they were in opposition to the allied cause.
That is right.

We are now told by the minister that certain investigations have been made, and that after those investigations these persons have been admitted to Canada. So far as I am concerned, the minister's explanation is nothing at all. If the situation is that people can be admitted

to this country against our laws, and the minister speaking for the government can then say, "We made an investigation and they are entitled to be here; but we will not tell you what that investigation was"-well, that is exactly the minister's position, and I say there is something not only rotten but thoroughly rotten in the state of Denmark, and even in the state of Canada.

Following up what the hon. member has said, let me tell him that in the last few months we have had refugee ships coming to this country from Sweden. They have carried refugees with not a document on them. May I ask him if he would insist that, because they have no documents on them, we should require that they be returned to the country from which they came?
Oh, no.
You said that.

I agree with you entirely. I read all about those people. They came in ships supposed to hold fifteen people, but sixty-five or eighty-five were loaded into them. But the people the hon. member for Winnipeg North is talking about did not come that way. These people came and threw themselves on our mercy-the people you are talking about who came in the ships. But the other people came with forgeries to back their admission. That is a different situation altogether. I said "forgeries" and I mean it -forged passports.
You may be right-and I hope you are right, because I like you; I like everything about you-but on the other hand do not permit yourself, Mr. Minister, to get into a position of concealing facts which began with fraud. I do not know anything about those people. But I do know that when a man enters this country on a forged passport, even though he may have come in a suite on the Queen Mary, he has no right to be here. He may be able to do that, even though he may have an excellent name-and I have forgotten this particular name. He may have a splendid name, or may be even a count. In those circumstances I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North is entitled to know what the facts are which permit you, Mr. Minister-and I say this with the greatest respect in the world-to set aside the law and to admit this person or other persons.
In the first place it was not I who set aside the law, as the hon. member has said. There was no law set aside by anyone.

An order in
council.

I was not
here at the time, but-
Forgive me; I was not speaking of you as an, individual. I know you are far above the cabinet level, and that you would never break the law.

When it is suggested that because someone had a passport that is not in order, he must be a criminal, that does not follow. After the war, as is well known, European countries were pretty well upset and, in order to escape from the countries in which they were living, some people obtained any kind of document procurable. That circumstance did not condemn a man when he arrived in this country.
Agreed.

We then investigated their background. The result of the investigations was submitted to government authority, who decided that certain individuals should be allowed to remain in Canada, and others should be sent out. Naturally, the source of the information cannot be made public, and I cannot give the details of it.
I do not want the source; I want to know what they found.

They found they were all right.
Mr. Gibson (Hamilton West:) They found they were not collaborators who should be sent back.

May I
take it that a person who comes to this country, having been accused and convicted of a criminal offence in another country, a friendly country, is perfectly in order in coming here to stay? Is that not in violation of the immigration law? Does that law not say, in part, that these individuals must be of good character; and does not the minister know that these men were convicted of criminal offences in France?

No, I do not
admit that they were convicted of crime. There were trials held in absentia. They had not a chance to defend themselves; and, although judgments may have been rendered against them, that does not prove they were guilty of crime or of the charges which had been laid against them.

I point out that they had every chance to defend themselves-even asked to go back to France to defend themselves.

And you know what would happen to them if they went back, whether they were guilty or not.

What
would happen? May I put it the minister meant that these men would be liquidated if they went back to France?

One gets a bit tired sitting here listening to members who talk the way the hon. member is talking, and the way the hon. member for Calgary West was talking a few moments ago, suggesting that members of the government are not acting in accordance with the law. Anyone who has come from the old land, as my hon, friend has, knows that for ages the greatest refuge for political prisoners has been Great Britain. Great Britain never has sent anyone back to the country from which he came because of a political crime that might be charged against him and that might result in a sure sentence of death.
About the end of the war these men left Europe and came to this country. Every man who came to this country under those circumstances was properly screened. I have no hesitation in saying that as one of the members of the government I was responsible along with every other member of the government for the orders in council that were passed. Those orders in council took into consideration the fact that there had been a proper screening of these people in so far as we were able to screen them. We decided finally that some should remain here and that some should go back to where they had come from. I hope that all the decisions were made on exactly the same basis as British practice has made its decisions over the years, namely, that you do not send a man back to sure death at the end of a war because of political differences that may have existed in the country from which he came. If we made any mistakes, I hope we made them on the side of mercy.
I can assure the Minister of Agriculture that I am completely tired of his irrelevancies; when he attempts to answer a question he skates around it in every possible way.
It is the only answer that could be made to the question and the only one which would agree with long-time practice in Britain or any other free democracy.

The Minister of Agriculture has suggested that if these men go back to a friendly, democratic country which was and is an ally of ours and which will be an ally of ours again, they will be

Supply-Mines and Resources liquidated. The French ambassador to this country has made it known quite amply and clearly that if these men go back to France they will get a fair and free trial. I have placed on the record tonight the number of death sentences which were carried out in France and which were less than one per cent of those convicted. I claim that these men had no right to come to this country, that they entered illegally and have been kept here illegally.

I should like to ask a question with regard to the money collected from those people who came back on the exchange ship Gripsholm from the Orient during the war. I believe that comes under his department.
Would my hon. friend bring that up under the immigration item later on when the official will be here?
The money was collected by the immigration branch?

805. Maintenance of plant of Abasand Oils Limited, $85,000.
These oil sands have been discussed in the house year after year and I think we should have an up-to-date report from the minister as to what the developments have been in the last year.

Abasand Oils Limited was wound up and during the period before it was finally wound up the company had maintained equipment and property on the location at a cost of $85,000. Have the tar sands operations been abandoned? On many occasions we have been told that these sands constitute one of the world's great oil reservoirs and it would be disappointing to know that these tremendous natural resources are being abandoned.

I would not say that the resources are being abandoned by any means, but the development has been suspended for the present. There has been such a tremendous development of cheaper oils that it is not considered advisable to go ahead with this development at the present time.
What has been the total expenditure in the last ten years, say, or the total to date in connection with the development of exploitation by Abasand?
It will be in the neighbourhood of a million and a half dollars.

I would point out that the United States government is hard-surfacing that part of the Alaska highway that lies within the borders of Alaska, and the time might very well come when that portion within our own borders will be hard surfaced. In that case material from Aba-sand might be profitably used.

When the dominion government ceased to support any experimentation in connection with the McMurray oil sands, in which this Abasand company was engaged, I believe the Alberta government continued to work on that project. As a matter of fact I understand that last year they spent between a half and three-quarters of a million dollars on it. I should like to ask the minister if the dominion government turned over to the province of Alberta any of the plant that was built there, or any of the data it obtained as a result of the four or five years of work carried on with dominion government funds.

Was there any turnover to the Alberta government of information obtained as a result of the experiments carried on by the dominion government?
Of course our officials are in collaboration with the officials of the Alberta government on that work; but there was no turning over of equipment to them.
In this case I did not ask about the equipment; I asked about turning over data and information.
Oh, there is the closest co-operation between the mines branches of the province and the dominion on all information that is obtained.

Item agreed to.
Eastern Rockies forest conservation board-
184.	To provide for the salaries and expenses of dominion members of the board and their alternates and sundry expenses in connection with the maintenance and operation of the Ottawa office of the board, $23,000.

This particular project in connection with the conservation of the eastern slope of the Rockies I believe is one


of the most valuable undertakings the government has initiated, and I should like the minister to tell us in a general way briefly what has been accomplished so far with respect to restoring the forest cover on the eastern slope of the Rockies, thereby conserving moisture and the flow of the streams which lead down to all the prairie provinces.

As hon. members know, this board which looks after the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains was set up by act of parliament. It consists of two representatives of the dominion government and one of the province of Alberta. The board receives funds each year from the dominion government, in addition to certain capital advances running over a period of six years. It is taking steps to conserve the slopes of the Rockies by providing roads and fire stations in that area, so the forests may be protected; it has power to make recommendations, and is responsible for the work that is being carried out.

I know all that; I knew it when I asked the question. I asked what has been done, in other words what are the results? What roads have been built? What fire stations have been established? Just what has been accomplished in the year and a half or so this board has been in operation?

It is difficult to give all the details, but I can give a summary of some of them. For example, the contract work was confined to the main north and south road through the conservation board area, which with the exception of some thirty-one and a half miles has now been graded from Coleman, Alberta, to the southern boundary of the dominion forest experimental station in the Kananaskis river valley. The road is being built with a traffic surface twenty feet wide, the width of side ditches being additional. In high fills the road is being built twenty-two feet wide, to provide for sloughing and erosion. The New West Construction Company of Edmonton have completed 44-2 miles on their contract north from Coleman, at an average cost of $10,082 per mile. This figure only includes bridge work and bridge materials installed to the 14th November, and covers some thirty per cent of the bridge piers and abutments with no bridge superstructure being completed.
On the Kananaskis section, southerly over the Pocaterra summit the Assiniboia Engineering Company, contractors, have partly completed the grading of 31 -5 miles at an average cost per mile of $12,812, which includes the

cost of all concrete bridge abutments and the material therein. No superstructure costs are included.
It is the view of the board on analysing these costs that at least $3,000 per mile has been saved on these grading operations by the award of contracts on a unit price basis for various items of work, rather than on a cost plus fixed fee basis.

Do I understand from what the minister has said that all this board has accomplished so far is the construction of a certain amount of highway near Canmore, and the construction of a few bridges to the north, less superstructure?

No, I would not say that was the only work by any means.
I would be very glad to let the hon. member have a list of what has been done in connection with fire stations and other bits of work that have been undertaken or that are in progress. I have not all the details before me, but I should be glad to let him have the list if he so desires.

Has any decision been made as to whether through trucking will be allowed in the national parks which may be on the route of the trans-Canada highway?

No decision has been made because we do not know where the trans-Canada highway will go. We do not encourage through trucking on the roads in the parks.

Supply-Mines and Resources

Surely a decision could be made as a matter of principle. The trans-Canada highway is practically bound to go through one of the national parks, if not more. It has been decided to assist in the development and building of the trans-Canada highway. Surely as a matter of principle it should have been decided whether or not through trucking is to be permitted in the parks- whether it be Yellowstone park, Jasper, Banff or the one on the southern route between Alberta and British Columbia. One of them will be involved. Have we not yet any decision as to whether through trucking will be allowed, and whether adequate roads will be provided?
I do not think that question has been taken up with the national parks service.
Why?
I have no doubt some decision will be reached, but I have not heard of the matter having been brought up.

I would suggest that the minister make inquiry about it, because I know the government of British Columbia is much concerned about this question as it affects the trans-Canada highway. They have not yet been able to get any assurance from the dominion government that there will be adequate facilities for trucking through the national parks. This is an important question in British Columbia, and I am surprised the minister has not had any word of this difficulty. As a matter of fact it has already restricted trade between British Columbia and Alberta to a large extent, and I think without reason.

The negotiations have been carried on with the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. Certainly we have had nothing passed on to us-at least, so far as I know-as to any negotiations in regard to trucking through the parks.

authorities looking over the area. No decision has yet been reached as I do not think the report has come in.

If the minister wants more details about this I can give them, but I think this is something in administration which has just been overlooked but which should be corrected immediately. I cannot see any justification for charging a coal dealer, or any other dealer, this fee every time he goes to get a load. The revenue would be nothing, but it is rather tough on the fellow who is selling coal. I am not asking the minister to say tonight that it will be stopped, but I wish he would look into it. I have no doubt that it is something that has been inherited in the administration.
The minister's predecessor was a great personal friend of mine and I do not know just how to refer to him. He has gone to another place and I hope no one will regard that as meaning that he has gone to the bourne from whence no traveller returns-he has gone to the Senate. Dominion wildlife service-
222.	Wildlife resources conservation and development, including administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, $259,520.

I understand the migratory birds act officials have jurisdiction over the setting of the season for ducks in the fall. This year it was set back from September 15 to October 15. I happen to be a duck shooter myself. I was out the first morning, and that was the first time I ever failed to get ducks. Sportsmen in our part of the country got absolutely none throughout the season, which was the worst we have ever had. I want to draw this to the attention of the minister in the hope that next year we might at least split the difference and have the season open October 1. By October 15 all the local ducks have departed for the south and the northern ducks have not yet come in. We feel that we are simply raising ducks and somebody to the south is shooting them.
These dates are set as the result of a conference held with all the provinces, and the provinces were unanimous on the dates set this year.
Then the provinces were absolutely astray as far as eastern Ontario was concerned.

In spite of all the scowls coming my way I am going to say a word on this item, even though it is late. There is an increase in this item of $38,020. I believe it is most important that we do everything possible to conserve wildlife, as well as to conserve the top soil, our forest resources, and such things as those. Down in Renfrew county we have an opportunity to do something in the way of conserving wildlife. We have a farmer named Harry Berry, who lives some ten miles west of Carleton Place on highway 17. Some twenty-five years ago seventeen wild geese landed on his farm and stayed for about six weeks. He did not disturb them but protected them, and they have been returning in greatly increased numbers

Supply-Mines and Resources each year since that time. Last spring some eight thousand wild geese landed on his farm.
It is now getting too much for one farmer to feed these increasing numbers of geese. Eight thousand wild geese can pull a lot of young clover out of the fine soil on Harry Berry's farm, and now he is asking for some assistance. When so many millions of dollars can be spent in our parks to attract tourists, why not spend at least something to help this man feed these geese? They have not only been eating his clover; he has been feeding them grain out of his granary all these years, and I believe he deserves some kind of help. I am asking the minister now to give consideration to some assistance for this man, and also to consider setting aside this territory along Muskrat lake as a bird sanctuary.
I have taken up this matter with the minister personally, and I think he knows the situation there. Muskrat lake is perhaps ten miles long and does not average more than a mile in width; it is really an extension of the Muskrat river. Ninety-eight per cent of the farmers owning land along Muskrat lake have signed a petition asking the minister to have this property set aside as a bird sanctuary, and that petition is supported by at least five reeves of the district. We feel that this is important, and we would like the matter settled before the geese come back next spring, when there will be probably ten thousand. So I am placing the matter before the minister tonight in the hope that he will not overlook it in the interval.

It has not
been the policy of the federal government to establish bird sanctuaries under the Migratory Birds Convention Act without prior consent from the provincial government concerned. The matter of this proposed sanctuary was taken up promptly with the provincial department of lands and forests, but that department wished to further study the situation. At the moment an investigation is being carried out by the dominion wildlife officer for Ontario and an officer of the Ontario department of lands and forests.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Will the minister give us some details of the agreement between the federal government and the province of

Manitoba in regard to this road from The Pas to Flin Flon? What was to be the total cost, and how much was paid?

The purpose of this vote is to provide for the dominion contribution to the cost of section B Cranberry Portage to Cuprus mines, of the proposed road between The Pas and Flin Flon in Manitoba, in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the dominion and the province of Manitoba dated September 30, 1948.
The increase in the dominion contribution is in accordance with the terms of the agreement, wherein it was proposed to expend $100,000 in 1948-49; $305,000 in 1949-50; and the balance in 1950-51.
The agreement provided for the work on the road to be started not later than April 1, 1948, and completed on or before September 30, 1950. The road is to be an all-weather standard gravel surface with sufficient width for two-way traffic. Work commenced early in 1948 and at the end of the calendar year, approximately 17 miles of clearing, 10 miles of grading, and 10 miles of gravelling were completed. The Pas-Flin Flon highway will be approximately 95 miles in length, of which 27 miles between Cuprus mines and Cranberry Portage are in a potential mineral belt. The total dominion contribution will be $437,000.

I should like to ask the minister when the new Indian Act will be brought forward?
I would say the next session of parliament.
I had a few remarks I wanted to make in that connection.

Make them tomorrow
morning.

I would rather make them right now. The minister will remember that there was a joint committee of this house which sat for three years revising this Indian Act. After the completion of the draft revision, it was sent to the Department of Justice so that the officers of that department could look it over. During the spring session of this

parliament, several members asked when the revised Indian Act would be introduced. Invariably, the answer has been that it was still in the hands of the Department of Justice officers. That excuse got so thin that I think the minister himself was ashamed to put it forward.
In answer to the member for Brant-Went-worth, the minister has suggested that the act will be introduced next year. Have the Department of Justice officials completed their lengthy consideration of this act? It has been in their hands since June, 1948. Will the act, as revised by the committee and with all the changes made by the Department of Justice, be the act introduced, or will the joint committee on Indian affairs be reconstituted for further work in this connection?

As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister spoke on this subject the other day. He pointed out that the Indian Act would not be introduced in this session, but would be left over until the next session. The report of the Indian affairs committee was a good report. My department worked to incorporate certain proposals for amendments to the act, and they were all sent down to the Department of Justice. When the act arrived at the Department of Justice, it was found it was a long time since it was overhauled, and that department felt there were other amendments which should be put in, quite apart from those recommended by the committee. Under those circumstances, the bill has not come back from justice yet. I understand it will not be ready until the next session.

Really, that is complete nonsense. This committee sat for three years considering the matter, and had the benefit of advice from solicitors from the Department of Justice as to what should be in the act, and what should not be in the act; what would work, and what would not work. This story that the Department of Justice found out the act had not been revised for many years is ridiculous, because the reason for setting up the committee in 1946 was that the act had not been revised since the nineties. Everybody knew that. The minister now says that the Department of Justice found out it had not been revised for many years, and yet the chief reason the committee was set up was to revise the act.
As I say, we spent three years in revising the act, and in addition a royal commission was appointed which spent considerable time travelling through the eastern portion of this country. After all this work was done, and after all this advice had been received from
Supply-Mines and Resources the Department of Justice officials, the minister now gets up and says that the Department of Justice found out the act had not been revised for a long time, and has, therefore, been holding it for this length of time.

I just want to correct my hon. friend in one respect. There was no representative from the Department of Justice on that committee. I understand there were solicitors from the Department of Mines and Resources, but not from the Department of Justice.

Naturally, the Department of Justice did not have representation on the committee, because the committee was composed of members of the House of Commons and the Senate. The Department of Justice did send representatives over to advise the committee, including Mr. Varcoe. The point I am getting at is that the government has been absolutely negligent in the matter of looking after this promised revision of the Indian Act. I do not think they can put forward excuses any longer for not taking action on the matter.
There are one or two other specific matters to which I should like to refer. The first is concerned with the fishing rights of Indians in the province of Alberta. The Indians were granted fishing rights in the various lakes in that province by treaty. The fish constituted one of their main items of food. Last year an order in council was passed by this government, apparently as a result of representations made by the government of Alberta, which prevented the Indians from doing any fishing in those lakes, except on Wednesdays or Thursdays, I think; it was one day a week. I suppose it was Thursday the idea being that the Indians could then have fish for Friday.
Often there were storms on Thursdays, or the fish were running on the opposite sides of the lake to that on which the Indian was fishing, or something of that nature happened, which meant the Indian had no fish. I should like to ask the minister what steps have been taken by his department to get this order in council rescinded, or to make some agreement with the Alberta government which will allow these Indians their treaty rights. I have made representations to the department about this matter.

When the natural resources were turned over to the province in 1930, under the agreement it left the Indians with ordinary rights for fishing and trapping in the province. There has been no change in that situation.

Supply-Mines and Resources

That is absolutely wrong. Nothing affected these fishing rights until last year, when an order in council was passed by this government limiting the right of the Indians to fish in these lakes to one day a week.

I understand that the Indians are subject to the laws of the province. I do not know of the order in council to which my hon. friend is referring that took away any rights that they had up to last year.
If the minister does not know he had better consult the officials in the Indian affairs branch and find out.
They do not know either.

They know about it. I have had correspondence with them on the matter. The order in council was passed in the last year. It is very recent and was passed as a result of representations from the Alberta government, again I think because of representations made to them by the fish and wildlife association of Alberta. The actual effect of this order in council is that the Indians bordering on these lakes have been deprived of their treaty rights which were guaranteed to them by the treaties which were signed when this territory was taken over from them. In addition to that, they have been deprived of their means of livelihood. The result of their being prevented from fishing is that the taxpayer of Canada has to provide them with welfare funds, food and so forth.

The special fishery regulation to which my hon. friend is referring is, I understand, one that was passed by the province of Alberta. As I said before, when the natural resources were taken over by the provinces it left the provinces with the right to regulate the use of the natural resources of the provinces. That I think must be the regulation to which my hon. friend is referring.
I think the minister will find that an order in council was passed by his own government, which is the one to which I am referring. I have had correspondence-
An order in council was passed approving the fishery regulation of the province of Alberta.
Yes.

I find that was passed, but that is only approving of the regulation that had been passed by the province of Alberta.
[Mr. Gibson (Hamilton West) .1

That is one of the things that I complained about. The minister is supposed to be the guardian of the Indians and is supposed to look after their rights. Instead of safeguarding their fishing rights in these lakes, as a matter of fact, the government passes an order in council giving away the rights. That is the very thing I am complaining about.

I want to support the hon. member in his request that a new Indian Act be brought down. Members of the parliamentary committee worked three years on the proposed act. As he has already said, they were turned into a royal commission and toured a part of this country. The proposed act they brought down was probably one of the most progressive pieces of legislation offered to this house on behalf of a group of people in this country. Because the Indian Act is obsolete the record of our own country regarding Indian affairs has been far from satisfactory and far from a credit to Canada. When the proposed act was recommended by the committee in the report to this house we all hoped that it would be something of a charter for the Indians in order that they might be encouraged to find a place in the life of Canada. I think the committee did an excellent job and produced an equally excellent report. We had the makings of a very good Indian Act.
Like the hon. member, I do not see why it takes a year and a half to refer this matter to the Department of Justice for other suggestions and amendments. Because the act has not been revised for a good many years, surely the Department of Justice should have been interested in the act at the same time as the committee was sitting and discussing Indian affairs. I think it is a shame that after three years of work, and the approval of the proposed act which had the makings of something good for the Indians and for Canada herself, nothing had been done with it.
The criticisms made by the hon. member are fully justified. I was not a member of the committee, but I followed it very closely. Several members of our party were on the committee. I saw the work they did; I saw the work that was done by members of other parties, including hon. members on the government side of the house in the last parliament. They worked effectively; they worked well; they worked conscientiously to do something for the Indians of this country. The least that could be done would be to bring legislation before the house early in the next session and not allow anyone anywhere to interfere with or circumvent the wishes of the committee which made such an excellent report to the house.

I have one more question in connection with welfare payments paid to aged Indians. Indians are the only people in this country who are not eligible for old age pensions. The welfare payments made to aged and other indigent Indians are now at the rate of $7.80 per month. The Indian association of Alberta has made representations to the Indian affairs branch to raise this amount to at least $15 a month. This afternoon in discussing medical matters as far as the Indians were concerned, the Minister of National Health and Welfare agreed that one of the reasons why tuberculosis and other diseases are so much more evident among the Indians than in the rest of the population is dietary deficiencies. I suggested to him that perhaps one of the best things he could do in order to improve the health of the Indians would be to recommend to the government that they increase the scale of these welfare payments so as to provide at least something reasonable in the way of money or payments in kind with which Indians could feed themselves decently. I urge the minister, who is directly responsible for this, that these welfare payments be increased. I think everyone will agree that the present scale is ridiculously low.

I think I should point out that in addition to the $8 that they get for welfare they also get subsistence in the form of fuel, clothes, food and medical attention in addition to the cash payments that they receive. Therefore it is not just the money alone.
Treaty or non-treaty Indians?

The minister says that they get these things in addition. If he will look into it he will find that the amount of food they get in addition to the welfare payments is very small. It amounts to a certain quantity of meat, in many instances meat that could not otherwise be sold, cast-off meat, and flour and a few other items along that line. It does not amount to very much. I have forgotten the money value of it. I think it is a very small amount.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I had occasion to refer to conditions of health among the Indians in the Rocky Mountain House district of Alberta. I was greatly pleased witih the response that came from the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Tonight for just one brief moment I should like to point out that in order to solve the problem which I brought up this afternoon it will be extremely necessary for officials of the Indian affairs branch to give serious and thoughtful consideration to the responsibilities
Supply-Mines and Resources that rest upon them in connection with this problem. We have approximately 200 Chippewa Indians who have not come under the treaty. A tremendous amount of ground work was done in that district by old-timers in the district. I mentioned one this afternoon, Mr. Henry Stelfox. The Indians were practically at the point where they were prepared to accept treaty, and then the Indian affairs department sent a man in to negotiate with them. I believe that my ten-year-old boy would have been just as competent to deal with these Indians-I will not mention any names-as this gentleman. He was not even civil with the Indians, with the result that this advance party which had come down to discuss treaty turned and went back in disgust. It is not beyond the realm of possibility to get these Chippewa Indians into treaty. But some care must be exercised in the type of man who goes in there to negotiate with them.
I would stress one or two points in connection with this. Whether it happens to be the agent or someone else located at Rocky Mountain House, this person must be essentially of a very humane character. He must be one who has the interests of those Indians at heart. He must know something of the history of those Indians. He must know something about the nature of the country in which they live.
I have not met the agent or the officials at the agency at Rocky Mountain House. I am not going to register any complaint about them, but I am going to stress upon the minister that he be certain above all else that he has the right man in there, if he ever expects to get those 200 Chippewa Indians into the treaty. I suggest the attention of his officers should be focused upon that situation to determine whether or not the right man is in charge at that agency.
With respect to the Crees who are on the reservation at that point, let me say that on that reservation there is a large quantity of timber-sufficient, if properly dealt with, to provide a great deal of security for those Indians over a long period of time. On the basis of the information I have received I am fearful that situation is not being dealt with properly. For example, these Indians should be allowed to go in there and establish their own small mill. It does not cost much money. Let it be all Indian labour, and let them take out their own timber under supervision.
Today the policy seems to be to let the white man go in there and establish his own mills, with the result that the poor Indian gets nothing but the wages paid to him-and sometimes those wages are not very high.

I do not think he did.

If the Indian affairs branch is charged, with custody of the Indians, and we appropriate money for the welfare of those Indians, why is it that that branch of government does not know anything about the health of the Indians in its custody? Perhaps this is one reason why the Indian population is in such an unsatisfactory condition today, and why our Indians have not


been raised to the level of the white population, as the natives of some other countries have been raised to the level of the white population there.
Because of the division of power, if we may so describe it, among the various branches of government it would seem that this condition has arisen. The same applies to education. What are the educational levels among the Indians? How is that education looked after? What kind of schools have they? To what extent are they educated? I have been to some of these Indian schools, and I will say that in the junior grades I found that the level was about the same as that of white children. I know something about this, because at that time I was supervising schools and knew something about educational levels.
But a little later on there seemed to be no provision for higher grades in the schools, no provision for higher education among them. We know perfectly well that, given the opportunity, the Indian has the same mentality as other people, and can be raised to the level of the whites.
That is one of the reasons I want to see this Indian Act brought down. That is one of the reasons I want to see a complete revision of the provisions for education, health and everything else in the Indian affairs branch. This thing is a public scandal in Canada, and it is a scandal that the government has not brought down the act for revision, so that we may do something about it.

May I say
that we are just as anxious to have the act brought down as other members of the house. With regard to the health of Indians, I am informed that the health has been improving. Certainly the birth rate is the highest of any group in this country. They are increasing rapidly.
But what is the infant mortality rate?
